US President Donald Trump's approval rating was stuck at the lowest level of his political career amid broad dissatisfaction over the war in Iran and the Republican's economic stewardship, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that concluded on Monday.
Just 33% of Americans approve of the job Trump is doing in the White House - the third straight Reuters/Ipsos poll with that share of respondents giving the president a thumbs up.
Trump's political brand looks increasingly like a potential weight on his Republican Party, which will be defending slim congressional majorities in the November 3 midterm elections.
Democrats appear more fired up about the elections, with 46% of self-identified Democrats describing themselves as "very enthusiastic" about voting in November, compared to 31% of Republicans, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll which surveyed 1,167 US adults nationwide.
Asked which party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today, 36% of independents in the survey picked Democrats and 22% said Republicans.
Trump popularity rating remains below Joe Biden low point
Since mid-August, Trump's popularity has held at a level it only briefly touched early in his first presidency, and well below the 47% share of Americans who approved of his performance early in his current term. His rating is lower than the low point his predecessor in office, Democrat Joe Biden hit, at 35% approval, in October 2024.
Like Biden, Trump has been dogged by widespread discontent over high levels of inflation. Gasoline prices have surged since Trump ordered the US to start bombing Iran in February, and just 36% of Americans approve of the war, the Reuters/Ipsos poll showed.
The conflict has had long lulls over the period, but in recent days the two sides have traded missile strikes and since the war's outset Iran has largely blocked a major transit point for the global oil trade.
Some 71% of Americans - including four in 10 Republicans - disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living. For the last month, registered voters in the survey have been saying the Democratic Party has better ideas for the economy than the Republican Party, the first time Democrats have led on the issue in about a decade.
The four-day poll had a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction.

Amazon.com illegally raised prices for advertisers by surreptitiously raising the minimum price required to place ads that promote their products, the US Federal Trade Commission alleged in a lawsuit filed in federal court Monday.

US steps up purchases of key Russian commodity – trade official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
21:34:17 UTC
06:34:17 KST

US steps up purchases of key Russian commodity – trade official
The US has stepped up purchases of Russian fertilizers despite broader Western restrictions on Moscow, with shipments rising by nearly a quarter in the first half of 2026, according to the Russia’s Export Center.
Veronika Nikishina, the center’s head, told RIA Novosti on Monday that the overall distribution of fertilizer exports had changed little since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. The US now ranks third among destinations for Russian supplies, she said, while Western Europe remains a larger market despite a decline in shipments this year.
Russia is the world’s largest exporter of fertilizers and one of the biggest producers, making its supplies difficult to replace on international markets. Fertilizer exports from the country were not directly targeted by Western sanctions, although broader restrictions on banking, shipping, and insurance have complicated trade. Moscow has meanwhile redirected a larger share of deliveries toward BRICS nations and the Global South.
“Sanctions against Russian fertilizers could have devastating consequences because of their importance to global food security. Even hardliners in unfriendly countries understand this,” Nikishina said.
US customs data cited by RIA in July showed that American fertilizer imports from Russia reached a record $1.04 billion between January and May, up 28% from a year earlier. Russia was the second-largest supplier to the US over that period after Canada, the figures showed.
In 2022, Washington authorized transactions involving Russian agricultural commodities including fertilizers to reduce the risk of shortages. The EU by contrast began imposing additional tariffs on some Russian nitrogen fertilizers in July 2025 as part of its drive to reduce reliance on Moscow, with the levies due to rise to €430 ($500) per ton by 2028.
The US-Israeli war on Iran and the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz have further exacerbated pressure on global fertilizer markets. The waterway handles an estimated third of the world’s fertilizer trade and a fifth of LNG shipments – a key input in the production of nitrate fertilizers. Experts, including Heartland Institute adviser Jeff Stier, have warned that any simultaneous disruption in the strait, the Black Sea, and to supplies from other major producers could trigger shortages of crop nutrients and a delayed food-price shock.

India needs to make up its mind about economic ties with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
21:30:06 UTC
06:30:06 KST

Advertisement
India needs to make up its mind about economic ties with China
New Delhi’s approach has gone from welcoming economic engagement with Beijing to containment to the latest calibrated reopening
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
As India prepares for the Brics summit less than two weeks away, relations with China are warming up. On July 22, Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi during the East Asia Summit; five days later, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri visited China. Last week, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval also visited Beijing, for border talks.
But India remains deeply ambivalent when it comes to economic engagement with China: it seeks Chinese capital, technology and expertise while fearing the shocks they may bring. Justifying the latest economic engagement with China, Jaishankar said India’s long-term objective was to compete with China in manufacturing.
After six years of sweeping curbs on Chinese investment, bilateral trade rose to US$151.1 billion in the financial year ended March 31. China remains India’s largest import source and has, after four years, displaced the United States as its top trading partner. India’s approach to engaging with China has evolved: from welcoming participation to containment after 2020 and, more recently, a calibrated reopening.
During Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first term and the early years of his second, India maintained a broadly open stance. Launched in 2014, the “Make in India” campaign sought to slash bureaucratic hurdles and attract foreign investment. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit that September, both sides signed a five-year economic cooperation plan. Modi’s 2015 China visit yielded a further US$22 billion in commercial deals.
Economic engagement remained robust even after the 2017 Doklam stand-off. Both sides maintained senior economic dialogue, pursued the “China India Plus One” approach to projects in third countries and planned connectivity projects. Chinese investment in Indian start-ups grew twelvefold between 2016 and 2019, backing at least 18 of India’s 30 unicorns. In 2019, China proposed a manufacturing partnership. By early 2020, the stock of Chinese investment in India was estimated to exceed US$26 billion.
But that was also the year the turning point came. In April, India introduced a requirement of prior government approval for foreign direct investment (FDI) from countries it shared a land border with, ostensibly to block “opportunistic takeovers”. After the deadly Galwan Valley border clash, restrictions against Chinese businesses expanded. India banned Chinese apps on national security grounds, tightened public procurement rules for bidders and required security clearance for directors from border countries. Visa delays, regulatory raids and other pressures suffocated Chinese business.

Han Liin Washington, DC
China’s biggest box-office surprise this year – a Teochew-language family drama that became a hit in Southeast Asia – is finally coming to North American cinemas on September 4.
Dear You, whose Chinese title translates as “Love Letters for Grandma”, has grossed nearly US$300 million in mainland China. Its North American release will test whether a Chinese film rooted in migration, family, and regional culture can find an audience beyond the Chinese-speaking diaspora.
The seemingly non-political film also sparked debate over China’s cultural influence among overseas Chinese communities, raising questions about the role Chinese cinema can play in shaping perceptions of China overseas, and whether that cultural reach can translate into soft power.
The film follows a debt-ridden grandson from the Teochew, or Chaoshan region of Guangdong Province, as he travels to Thailand to find the grandfather he believes abandoned his family, hoping the man behind years of qiaopi – letters sent by overseas Chinese migrants to their families, often accompanied by remittances – can help him repay his debts. He instead learns more about his family’s past and his grandparents’ relationship.
Its distributors hope its near-universal themes will transcend language and cultural barriers even as others are sceptical.
Bringing Dear You to the US
Dear You is being released by Well Go USA, a Texas-based, family-owned distributor focused on bringing Asian cinema to North American audiences.

India to witness above avg temperature in September; rainfall likely to be below normal
NEW DELHI: Monthly rainfall over the country as a whole is most likely to be below normal in Sept, the last month of the monsoon season, said IMD Monday - an indication that the four-month rainy season is likely to end with overall deficient cumulative rainfall, as was predicted earlier due to the impact of El Nino.IMD said Aug, which reported a deficit of more than 16% in monthly rainfall in the country despite good rains in certain parts, was the warmest Aug in India since 1901, recording a mean temperature of 28.010°C.Region-wise, South peninsular India recorded its second-warmest Aug since 1901. East and northeast India recorded their third-warmest, while northwest India saw its fifth-warmest, Aug in 126 years.
So far, the country as a whole has reported a deficit of 14% in cumulative (June 1-Aug 31) rainfall, despite ‘normal’ rainfall in July. In June, the deficit was as high as 35%. Out of a total of 741 districts assessed for monsoon rainfall distribution, 312 (42%) received ‘below-normal’ rainfall and 38 districts (5%) reported large deficient rainfall till Aug 31.A forecast of ‘below-normal’ rainfall in Sept may lead to a deficit in overall kharif acreage. Though the sowing of most seasonal crops is almost complete, with a decline in acreage of nearly 2% compared with the corresponding period last year, low rainfall in Sept implies an increase in input cost due to farmers’ spending on irrigation of standing crops.
“Spatially, many parts of the country are likely to receive below-normal rainfall, but some areas of northwest, northeast, east, east-central and south-east peninsular India are likely to receive ‘normal to above-normal’ rainfall,” said IMD chief Mrutyunjay Mohapatra.
He said “strong El Niño conditions” are currently prevailing over the equatorial Pacific Ocean, with sea surface temperature remaining above normal across central and eastern equatorial Pacific. “These conditions are expected to strengthen further in the coming months,” said Mohapatra, hinting at its negative impact on Sept rainfall.El Niño is invariably associated with a weak monsoon and a harsh summer in India.At present, neutral Indian Ocean Dipole conditions prevail over Indian Ocean, which are likely to persist through Sept.This means that monsoon may not benefit from this climatic phenomenon as only positive IOD helps increase rainfall activities.

Trump vows to hit Iran ‘hard’ after first exchange of fire in weeks

Trump vows to hit Iran ‘hard’ after first exchange of fire in weeks
- US and Iran exchanged attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, raising fears of escalating conflict; Trump vowed to "hit them hard" in response.
- Iran's missile and drone strikes targeted US forces in Jordan and UAE, while Iran called for dialogue to resolve tensions.
- US continues economic pressure on Iran, aiming to cripple its economy, while Iran maintains its blockade of the strategic shipping lane.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump threatened on Aug 31 to hit Iran “hard” after the two foes traded fire for the first time in weeks, as his Treasury secretary vowed to keep up a pressure campaign aimed at hobbling Tehran’s economy.
After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the strategic Strait of Hormuz closed and the US persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
On Aug 30, the United States carried out strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran quickly retaliating by attacking US military targets in the Middle East.
The exchange raised fears of a return to major hostilities, with the US president vowing to respond.
“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump said, according to a Fox News reporter who spoke to him briefly. “There will be a response.”
The United States said it attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak to prevent Tehran planting mines in the key shipping lane.
Iran responded with missile and drone attacks aimed at Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, saying they targeted US forces there, but President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Aug 31 called for dialogue.
“We continue to strive for a path of agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region,” he said at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, adding “the solution to the existing problems is dialogue and cooperation”.
State media reported that three people were killed in the US attack on Larak, with several others wounded.
Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards said the ballistic missile attack targeting two US air bases in Jordan caused “heavy damage”.
But Trump told Fox that all the missiles fired at US forces had been shot down, except for one that was determined not to pose a threat. Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.
Iran also said it targeted US personnel at an air base in the UAE, and shot down an American drone over Hormuz.
Abu Dhabi said it intercepted a drone over the country’s waters, but dismissed claims that Al Minhad Air Base had been targeted as “baseless”.
The Guards reported knocking out a second US drone over the Hormuz on the evening of Aug 31, and Iran’s armed forces central command reiterated a warning to its regional neighbours not to allow the US to use their territory to carry out attacks.
‘Continue exerting pressure’
The exchange of fire came after weeks of relative calm, with the Trump administration recently pivoting to “economic warfare”.
Earlier on Aug 31, Trump had called Iran “a Failed Nation”, saying on social media that its military was decimated, its finances were crumbling “and their leadership is in total disarray”.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowed to keep up the economic pain.
“We are going to continue exerting pressure, and we’ve had very good discussions here already,” Bessent told reporters at a G-20 meeting in North Carolina.
He said a turning point in the pressure campaign could come “within weeks or months”.
Iran is exerting economic pressure of its own through its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, which has roiled global markets and driven up prices for American voters in a closely fought midterm election year.
One-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait before the war, which was triggered by a surprise wave of US and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb 28.
Hormuz flashpoint
Despite traffic remaining throttled six months on, Trump has claimed the US navy has “total control” of the strait, with Washington last week announcing it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.
Iran, however, insists it is in charge of the sealane. The Revolutionary Guards said on Aug 31 that a “rogue” oil tanker caught fire near the strait after it hit two mines while attempting to transit an “illegal route”.
The US military called the claim “disinformation”, saying: “No ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz.”
Mediators have tried for months to broker an end to the war, but an earlier truce and memorandum of understanding fell apart.
Sporadic attacks resumed, but ultimately tapered off, with the US last striking Iran on July 29.
A spokesman for UN chief Antonio Guterres called the latest exchange of fire “very regrettable” after weeks of calm, and urged a return to diplomacy.
Iran recently has been trying to push the US to return to the previous deal, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi telling state TV on Aug 31 that “the solution is completely clear and straightforward: the United States must return to its commitments”.
“In that case, everything can be put back on the right track,” he said. AFP

'No plans' to deploy troops to midterm elections polling sites, top US general says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
21:20:57 UTC
06:20:57 KST

‘No plans’ to deploy troops to midterm elections polling sites, top US general says
- The top US general confirmed there are no plans to deploy federal troops or National Guard at polling sites during the 2026 midterm elections.
- Election security and administration remain the responsibility of state and local officials, with no military involvement in handling ballots or voting machines.
- Concerns about military interference arose after Trump suggested using troops to ensure election honesty, but federal law prohibits troops' deployment at polling places.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The top US general said the military has no plans to send federal military personnel or National Guard troops to polling places during 2026’s midterm elections.
In a letter to US Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat from Michigan, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine said election administration and security remain the responsibility of state and local officials.
Caine’s letter, which was obtained by Reuters, was sent in response to a request from Slotkin, who had sought assurances from senior military leaders, including Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, that the Trump administration would not interfere in the November elections.
While stressing that no such deployment is planned, Caine said the military has no plans to seize ballots, voting machines or other election-related material.
“I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections,” Caine wrote.
The letter was received Aug 28, according to an official.
Millions of Americans are due to vote on Nov 3 in congressional, gubernatorial and local elections.
Democrats, including Slotkin, have raised concerns that the Trump administration could seek to use troops or other armed federal personnel near polling places.
Those concerns were fuelled in part by comments Trump made in May when, asked whether he would send National Guard troops or Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to voting locations, he said he would “do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.”
Federal law generally prohibits the deployment of US troops at polling places or their use in overseeing elections, reflecting long-standing restrictions on military involvement in the electoral process. REUTERS

Ex-Israeli officials call West Bank settler violence 'ethnic cleansing'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
21:09:00 UTC
06:09:00 KST

Former senior Israeli military and security officials have condemned escalating settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, with some describing the campaign as "ethnic cleansing," The New York Times reported Sunday.
"This is ethnic cleansing, to put it simply,” retired Brig. Gen. Ephraim Sneh, who is also a former Israeli health minister, said of attacks on Palestinians, according to the newspaper.
Maj. Gen. Eyal Ben-Reuven, a former commander of Israel’s ground forces who also commanded a division in the West Bank, said occupier violence posed a greater concern to him than other security fronts.
"This, what the settlers are doing here, is the real threat to Israel,” Ben-Reuven said. "This is more concerning to me than Iran, Gaza or Lebanon.”
The comments came as retired Israeli generals and former senior officials have been touring Palestinian communities in the West Bank to examine the impact of occupier violence, including attacks on farmers and shepherds and the destruction of property.
Palestinian residents told the visiting officials they had lost access to their homes, farmland and grazing areas amid repeated attacks.
In the West Bank village of Burin, limping Palestinian farmer Bashar Eid said an occupier attack had left him permanently impaired and that repeated attacks prevented him from farming his land.
"I don’t know what to do,” Eid said. "They want to take my house.”
In the Jordan Valley, repeated attacks forced Palestinian families to leave the largely Bedouin encampments like Hamamat al-Maleh, according to the Times.
Only a few families remained when the Times visited in February after nighttime incursions forced most residents to flee, it said.
"We don’t even sleep an hour,” resident Mohammad Khalil, 37, said. "If they come and you’re asleep, you won’t survive it.”
By March, Khalil and the remaining families had also left following a series of raids, thefts and attacks, the newspaper reported.
In another Jordan Valley community, a Palestinian farmer said an occupier outpost and fencing had cut his family off from farmland and grazing areas.
"Six months ago, this was our land,” he said. "Now, it’s like a jail.”
More than 200 prominent Israelis signed a letter in June demanding an end to attacks against Palestinian civilians in the West Bank, according to the Times.
The signatories included two former prime ministers, more than 30 retired army and air force generals and former heads of Israel’s foreign and domestic intelligence agencies. Former officials, rabbis and other public figures also signed.
They called for an end to what they described as "Jewish terrorism” and "ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank.
The signatories also accused the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of pursuing "a deliberate government policy in which the entire security establishment - including the military, Shin Bet and the police - is knowingly complicit.”
They pointed to government funding for illegal Israeli settlement outposts and farms and demanded an accounting of public funds used to provide infrastructure and other support for them.
They also accused Israeli soldiers of sometimes standing by during attacks on Palestinians or participating alongside occupiers in assaults on Palestinian communities.
Moshe Ya’alon, a former Israeli army chief of staff and defense minister under Netanyahu, criticized extremist occupier ideology.
"What is Jewish supremacy?” Ya’alon said in remarks cited by the newspaper. "Eighty years after the Holocaust, ‘Mein Kampf’ in reverse. The master race is us.”
Asaf Agmon, a retired Israeli Air Force general who joined one of the tours, said efforts to remove Palestinians from parts of the West Bank reminded him of what Jews endured under Nazi rule. He stressed that he was not comparing the scale of the violence.
"Once a society behaves this way,” he said, "that society is doomed.”
Israeli occupiers have carried out thousands of attacks in the West Bank since October 2023, injuring thousands of Palestinians, according to UN figures cited by the Times.
According to UN figures cited by the Times, Israeli occupiers have carried out thousands of attacks in the West Bank since October 2023, injuring thousands of Palestinians.
More than 3,200 Palestinians have been displaced by occupier attacks so far this year, twice the rate recorded last year, while the average number of Palestinians injured in such attacks has risen from one every three days in 2020 to more than three per day in 2026, the report said.

No verdict after 3 days of deliberations in Lindsay Clancy trial over child killings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

No verdict after 3 days of deliberations in Lindsay Clancy trial over US child killings
Jurors at the Massachusetts court must determine whether the ex-nurse is criminally liable for killing her 3 children in 2023
Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial on Monday spent a third day deliberating without reaching a verdict on whether the former labour and delivery nurse is criminally responsible for killing her three children in 2023 – a case that has drawn attention to maternal mental health after childbirth.
The jurors began discussing the case on Thursday in Plymouth County Superior Court in Massachusetts after hearing testimony from more than 70 prosecution witnesses, including her former husband, and 10 defence witnesses over five weeks.
The jury is scheduled to resume deliberations on Tuesday.
While Clancy does not deny strangling her children, her lawyer said she did it because she had lost her grip on reality due to postnatal psychosis, a rare mental illness that can follow childbirth.
In the months before the killings, Clancy sought treatment for her worsening mental health, including a stay in a psychiatric hospital.
Prosecutors said Clancy knew what she was doing. They say she strangled the children because she was depressed and tired of living, and made a conscious choice to kill them before attempting suicide.
The jury could find her guilty of murder or the lesser crime of manslaughter, or it could acquit her if it finds that she was not in control of herself due to psychiatric problems.

Trump is considering limited strikes on Iran in the area of the Strait of Hormuz

Unknown Publisher

Trump is considering limited strikes on Iran in the area of the Strait of Hormuz
Kyiv • UNN
The United States may carry out limited strikes on Iranian positions near the Strait of Hormuz. The goal is to deter attacks on vessels and aircraft.
U.S. President Donald Trump and his advisers are considering the possibility of carrying out limited strikes on Iranian positions in the Strait of Hormuz area to prevent Tehran from restoring its capabilities to attack vessels. Axios reports this, citing informed sources, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the plan was developed by the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) and was also supported by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. Before the exchange of strikes between the United States and Iran that took place last weekend, Trump had not approved the plan.
At the same time, Axios sources say that a new escalation could prompt the U.S. president to give the "green light" for the operation. Its goal would be to reduce the risk of Iranian attacks on oil tankers, U.S. Navy ships, and American aircraft.
The U.S. is concerned about Iran restoring its capabilities
One U.S. official called the proposed strategy "mowing the lawn." It involves periodic limited strikes intended to prevent Iran from restoring its radar and missile capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz area.
According to U.S. officials, CENTCOM is concerned about Tehran's attempts to restore its military systems. One signal was the launch of an Iranian missile at an American F-35 fighter jet that was providing cover for vessels in the strait.
An Axios source said that the missile did not come close enough to the F-35 to pose a real threat. However, the U.S. regards the very fact of its launch as evidence that Iran is trying to restore its military capabilities.

HC reinstates bank official sacked without inquiry over hashtag campaign

J&K HC has set aside the dismissal of a bank executive sacked without an inquiry into an alleged #TortureKashmir hashtag campaign on social media
SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir high court has set aside the dismissal of a J&K Bank executive sacked without an inquiry into an alleged #TortureKashmir hashtag campaign on social media, ruling that a financial institution’s managing director “cannot be trusted with the drastic power to dismiss an employee without investigation”.“The President and governor are high constitutional functionaries and, therefore, they can dispense with the services of an employee without holding an inquiry in appropriate cases. But the same level of trust cannot be reposed in an officer of the level of managing director and CEO of a bank,” the single-judge bench of Justice Sanjay Dhar said in its verdict last Saturday.The petitioner, Saadut Hussain Pampori, joined J&K Bank as a computer engineer in June 1995 and rose to deputy general manager by 2022, serving as an officer on special duty to the chief minister from 2016 to 2018 under the BJP-PDP govt led by Mehbooba Mufti.The bank’s then MD suspended him on April 15, 2024, pending investigation into misconduct before ordering his dismissal on July 15 that year under Clause 12.29 of the officers’ service manual.The dismissal followed a report by DGP (CID) based on “credible sources, as also from discreet enquiries”. The report accused Pampori of spreading misinformation about alleged state-backed atrocities on Kashmiris.
The court held that information gathered from sources or through discreet enquiries by DGP does not qualify as an “investigation” under Clause 12.29, since the process involves no collection of evidence or recording of witness statements.
Justice Dhar drew a line between Clause 12.29 and Article 311(2)(c), under which govt may terminate an employee without the normal procedure if satisfied that retention is prejudicial to state security.J&K administration has dismissed nearly 100 govt employees under that provision.Clause 12.29, the court said, lays down specific preconditions, including an investigation by a state, Union territory or central agency, before an employee can be sacked.Quashing the order against Pampori as “not sustainable in law”, the court restored him to the post he held before his dismissal, albeit allowing the bank to proceed against him afresh.

Former French Prime Minister Edouard Balladur, technocrat who feuded with Chirac, dies at 97
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:50:45 UTC
05:50:45 KST

Former French Prime Minister Edouard Balladur, technocrat who feuded with Chirac, dies at 97
Aug 31 - After losing the 1995 presidential election against his ally-turned-rival Jacques Chirac, former French Prime Minister Edouard Balladur wrote: "Moved? No." He added: "I would not have been any more so had I won."
A stiff technocrat, Balladur was often portrayed by his critics as aloof and disconnected from his contemporaries' preoccupations. Plantu, a press cartoonist, sketched him as an aristocrat wearing a wig and seated in a sedan chair. The satirical weekly Le Canard enchaîné renamed him "His Courteous Smugness".
A leading figure of France's centre-right, Balladur was the architect of a sweeping privatisation drive that saw the sale of some of France's most prominent companies, including banks Société Générale and Paribas — later part of BNP Paribas — as well as broadcaster TF1. He also pushed through a reform of France's politically sensitive pension system in 1993.
Balladur played a crucial role in the early careers of several prominent politicians and businessmen, including former President Nicolas Sarkozy and billionaire Bernard Arnault's long-standing collaborator at luxury giant LVMH, Nicolas Bazire, who both worked for him during his 1995 run for office.
But that ill-fated campaign also caused lasting damage to his reputation, as courts scrutinised its financing. Following "a quarter-century of slander", as Balladur put it, he was finally cleared of any wrongdoing in 2021.
Balladur, the soft-spoken son of a banker, has died aged 97, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on X on Monday. No cause of death was given.
"Edouard Balladur is closely associated with fifty years of the history of the Fifth Republic. From his early days working alongside Georges Pompidou to his appointment as Prime Minister, he was a leading figure in our public life," Lecornu said.
Balladur was born in 1929 in the coastal city of Izmir, in what was then the Ottoman Empire, into a Christian family.
Though he was often said to be of Armenian origin, his name sometimes presented as a shorter version of "Balladurian", Balladur always denied it.
His family had been part of Izmir's French community for generations, his father being a director at the Ottoman Bank.
His parents emigrated with their six children in 1934 before settling in Marseille, in the south of France.
After graduating from the Ecole nationale d'administration, the training ground of France's bureaucratic elite, Balladur entered government in 1964 as an adviser to Prime Minister Georges Pompidou.
A decade later, he served as then-President Pompidou's chief of staff.
Stepping away from politics after Pompidou's death in 1974, Balladur returned to a far more powerful role in 1986, as economy, finance and privatisation minister in Chirac's centre-right cabinet during the first "cohabitation" (power sharing) with Socialist President François Mitterrand.
Balladur implemented Chirac's bold programme of cutting taxes and government spending, liberalising the labour market, lifting price controls, and reprivatising some of France's state-owned banks and industrial companies.
'I WAS NOT A VERY GOOD CANDIDATE'
As Chirac, scalded by his defeat in the 1988 presidential election, no longer wished to serve as prime minister, Mitterrand appointed Balladur to the role in 1993.
As head of the government, Balladur extended his privatisation programme. But as a lifelong admirer of the general-turned-president Charles de Gaulle, he remained wary of the untrammelled influence of free markets and the United States, arguing in 1993: "What is the market? It is the law of the jungle, the law of nature. And what is civilisation? It is the struggle against nature."
Chirac supported the bid by Balladur, his "friend of 30 years" whom he knew "better than anyone", for the premiership with the idea that he would pave the way for his own path to the presidency. Instead, Balladur emerged as the more popular of the pair and in 1995 announced his candidacy for the Elysee Palace, sparking a bitter rivalry between the two men.
In a television interview, Balladur had forcefully argued that a prime minister in a power-sharing government should not run for president. "If there is to be another cohabitation, it would be desirable, so that the climate is calmer and life more peaceful, for the prime minister not to be a candidate in the presidential election," he said.
"I do not see how a man could stand before the French people in 1993 and tell them I will not be a candidate in two years and then be one. That would be breaking his word."
Balladur's U-turn — and the fratricidal conflict with Chirac — did not at first seem to undermine his chances. He entered the race as the clear favourite.
"For the public, the presidential election is already decided," the French daily Le Monde headlined in January 1995, judging that polls showed Balladur's "uncontested dominance" "over all his competitors", while the International Herald Tribune asserted that Chirac appeared to have lost the struggle for his own party's loyalty.
Arlette Chabot, a news anchor of the public broadcaster France 2, went so far as to ask Chirac whether he might withdraw his candidacy, infuriating the politician.
As he recounted in his book "Deux ans à Matignon" (Two years in the prime minister's official residence), Balladur presented himself as the candidate of "reason" and "truth", focused on economic growth and fiscal responsibility against what he considered as the false promises of his competitors.
But the dynamics of the race shifted rapidly. Balladur struggled on the campaign trail, appearing uncomfortable as he engaged with voters. "I refused to make people dream," he said in 1995.
The election returned the centre right to power after two consecutive Socialist terms, but with Chirac, not Balladur.
He was eliminated in the first round of voting, winning 18.58% of the vote to Chirac's 20.84%. Decades later, in a 2016 documentary by Jean-Charles Deniau, he conceded: "I was not a very good candidate."
The career of Nicolas Sarkozy, Balladur's protégé, would be derailed for some time by his fierce support for the losing candidate, much of his party having come to see him as having also betrayed Chirac.
STAYING IN POLITICS
After that, Balladur retained a seat in parliament until 2007 and presided over the Foreign Affairs Commission at the National Assembly for five years. He was also appointed by Sarkozy, then France's president, as the head of two commissions, including one that inspired amendments to the French Constitution in 2008.
But his 1995 campaign lingered over the rest of his career. Beyond turning him into a secondary player in French politics, it also fed years of suspicion. Prosecutors argued that Balladur's run for office had been financed with 10.25 million francs of kickbacks derived from arms contracts with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed while he was prime minister. Charged with complicity in the alleged misappropriation of public funds, Balladur always denied any wrongdoing.
In France, the case was all the more sensitive because of a 2002 suicide bomb attack in the Pakistani city of Karachi, which killed 11 employees of French-owned naval shipbuilder Direction des constructions navales, and wounded 12 others. All were involved in building one of the submarines planned under the contract with Pakistan.
Several families of victims filed a complaint against Balladur, one line of inquiry in the case focusing on the attack potentially being motivated by the French government's alleged suspension of bribe payments to Pakistani officials.
In 2021, the Court of Justice of the Republic acquitted the former prime minister in what came to be known as the Karachi scandal, ruling that there was no evidence that he had personally ordered payments linked to the contract, nor sufficient proof to establish the origins of his campaign financing.
His former colleague and supporter during the campaign, ex-defence minister François Léotard, was sentenced by the same court to a two-year suspended prison term and a €100,000 fine for complicity in the alleged misappropriation of public funds. In January 2025, Balladur's former campaign director Nicolas Bazire was acquitted on appeal after being given a jail sentence by a lower court.
In late October 2025, Balladur was seen by AFP visiting Sarkozy on the eve of his brief imprisonment, unrelated to the Karachi case. At the end of that year, Balladur announced in Le Figaro newspaper the death of his wife of 68 years, Marie-Josèphe. They had four sons, Pierre, Jerome, Henry and Romain. REUTERS

Researchers defend older age of key archaeological site in Chile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:54 UTC
05:40:54 KST

Researchers defend older age of key archaeological site in Chile
Aug 31 - Two groups of researchers are defending the view that the Monte Verde archaeological site in Chile was occupied by ancient hunter-gatherers about 14,500 years ago after another study indicated it was much younger — a debate with major implications for understanding the initial peopling of the Americas.
This creek valley site, located in southern Chile about 36 miles (58 km) from the Pacific coast, was discovered in the 1970s. The scientific testing announced in 1997 that concluded that people were present at this locale deep in South America about 14,500 years ago suggested a much earlier arrival for humans in the New World than had been believed at the time.
But a study published in March based on different testing called that into question, concluding that Monte Verde dated to between about 4,200 and 8,200 years ago.
Now, the site's research team and another group of scientists have identified in analyses appearing in the journal PaleoAmerica what they consider fundamental flaws with that study, which was published in the journal Science.
"They did not demonstrate that the original geological interpretation of the site was in error," said Vanderbilt University anthropologist Tom Dillehay, who has studied Monte Verde extensively since the 1970s and led one of the analyses.
"I remain confident in our methodology and results," said University of Wyoming archaeologist Todd Surovell, who was the lead author of the research that suggested a younger age for the site — a finding that, if correct, would make Monte Verde irrelevant to the investigation of when people first spread through the Americas.
The older age would place Monte Verde more than 1,500 years before the previous earliest-known human occupation sites south of the continental ice sheets that covered parts of North America at the time. Those Ice Age sites were associated with North America's Clovis culture, known for distinctive stone tools and named for a locale in New Mexico.
Because Monte Verde was considered older and was thousands of miles south of the Clovis locations, scientists viewed it as evidence that people must have trekked into the Americas from Eurasia much earlier than the Clovis sites had indicated.
Dillehay faulted evidence presented by Surovell and colleagues as not arising from observations directly at the site where the archaeological evidence was found but instead from geology outside it.
An important element of the paper in Science was the description of a layer of volcanic ash deposited about 11,000 years ago that is situated below the archaeological evidence of occupation, which would show that the human presence at Monte Verde was more recent than that date.
"That was never observed by all investigators working at Monte Verde since 1977," Dillehay said of an ash layer.
Dillehay took issue with other aspects of the Science paper, and said he believes those researchers cherry-picked geological evidence to "fit a predetermined conclusion."
'A GREAT DEAL OF SCRUTINY'
Surovell said he welcomes continued scientific debate about the age of Monte Verde and the processes responsible for its formation. The best way to resolve these questions, Surovell said, is through additional study by independent researchers.
"Our work has now received a great deal of scrutiny, which is exactly what should happen with a claim this important. If there were major problems with our methods, data or reasoning, I would have expected them to become apparent through that process. So far, I have not seen criticisms that I think undermine the central conclusions of our study," Surovell said.
Dillehay underscored the archaeological importance of the site.
"Monte Verde's exceptional preservation has made it possible to recover materials rarely found in the archaeological record, including worked wood, remains of structures, plants, seaweed, and other organic materials, offering an extraordinary window into the life and knowledge of the human communities that inhabited southern Chile during the late Pleistocene," Dillehay said, referring to the geological timeframe spanning the last Ice Age.
Also found at the site were human footprints associated with a hearth, remains of fires, wooden tools and stakes, as well as remains of potatoes and animal bones and flesh.
"Monte Verde is well sealed by an anaerobic peat layer that preserved organics at the site, so we have a much more in-depth notion of the technology and especially the economy of people at that time. They were broad-spectrum consumers who lived on both plants and animals, and foraged from the Pacific coast to the Andean mountains," Dillehay said. REUTERS

Justice Department lawyers asked Mehta to order the emergency life-saving measures for Lakanwal.
“The defendant has medical capacity to make determinations regarding his health and he is refusing nutrition that is necessary to sustain his life,” they wrote.
Lakanwal’s lawyers said he would oppose the government’s request. They noted that he has consumed some food, such as apple sauce, while hospitalised but also has been “adamant at times” that he did not want to eat.
“At this juncture, the government does not indicate that Mr. Lakanwal’s condition is so dire as to require this Court’s intervention and the provided medical records do not support that position,” they wrote in a redacted court filing.

Farhad Ibragimov: Türkiye is one missile deal away from crossing Russia’s red line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:36:54 UTC
05:36:54 KST

Farhad Ibragimov: Türkiye is one missile deal away from crossing Russia’s red line
Recently, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that Moscow was still waiting for clarification from the US and Türkiye regarding possible arms supplies to Ukraine. Russia expects a response, as this matter directly affects not only bilateral relations but also the prospects for resolving the Ukraine crisis.
The issue goes far beyond the scope of yet another military-technical deal. In July, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan called for preventing the spread of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to the Black Sea region and advocated for the continuation of Ankara-mediated negotiations between Moscow and Kiev within the framework of the so-called Istanbul format. Türkiye emphasized that the security of shipping and energy infrastructure is of fundamental importance to it.
The Russian side, in turn, points out an obvious contradiction. According to Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Ankara and Washington, in their contacts with Moscow, stated that they sent Kiev signals about the unacceptability of attacks in the Black Sea. However, Moscow has not received a public or equally strong response from Türkiye and the US concerning Ukrainian drone strikes on commercial vessels and the infrastructure of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium near Novorossiysk. The Russian Foreign Ministry also warned that strikes on infrastructure and vessels used for delivering Western weapons to Ukraine would continue until the security threats in the region of the Azov and Black seas are eliminated.
Leaving diplomatic language aside, the question is very simple: can Türkiye simultaneously supply Kiev with weapons capable of being used against Russian targets and demand that Moscow continue to consider it a neutral intermediary?
What do the American documents actually state?
The US Congressional Record, published on August 6, shows two notifications about the proposed permanent transfer of American weapons from Turkish stockpiles to Ukraine. The first package includes 12 M270 MLRS launchers, 2,524 M26 unguided rockets with cluster munitions, and 47,000 M509A1 203mm cluster artillery shells. Their initial procurement price is listed at $255.9 million.
The second notification concerns 70 M39 ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles with an initial procurement price of approximately $28 million. In total this amounts to approximately $283.9 million. However, it would be incorrect to automatically assume that this is the price of the current contract since the terms of the potential deal between Ankara and Kiev have not been publicly disclosed.
Another point is equally important. The documents do not prove that the weapons have already been transferred to Kiev. They only confirm that the Turkish government proposed re-export, and the US Department of State notified Congress of its readiness to approve it after the statutory review period. Ankara cites the desire to get rid of outdated weapons and redirect funds toward modernizing its armed forces as the reason for the re-export. Kiev, according to the documents, intends to use these systems to enhance its offensive and defensive firepower.
This formulation makes the situation particularly serious. This isn’t about armored vehicles, communications equipment, or individual commercial drones; M39 ATACMS missiles are capable of engaging targets at ranges of up to 165 km and carry cluster munitions. Combined with M270 launchers and thousands of rocket and artillery munitions, this constitutes a comprehensive package of enhanced long-range firepower systems. Its possible use will inevitably entail losses among Russian troops and the risk of strikes deep into Russian territory.
Between mediation and participation
Russian-Turkish relations have never been an alliance in the strict sense of the word. Moscow and Ankara supported opposing sides in Syria and Libya; they hold different views on the status of Crimea, and compete for influence in various corners of Eurasia. Türkiye supplied Ukraine with drones, developed military-technical cooperation with it and consistently supported it. Yet, none of this prevented Russia and Türkiye from building gas pipelines, a nuclear power plant, developing trade, and reaching agreements in areas where their interests coincided.
This format was based on an unspoken rule that competition should not escalate into direct, critical damage to the other side. Strong disagreements could arise, but they remained manageable and were offset by cooperation in other areas.
The proposed transfer of ATACMS missiles, M270 launchers, and tens of thousands of cluster munitions brings Ankara dangerously close to the limits of this model of interaction. This is not a matter of one weapons system, but its purpose, the scale of the package, and the political context.
Türkiye isn’t simply offering to sell Kiev a batch of its own military equipment; it intends to transfer a large stockpile of American weapons intended to enhance Kiev’s firepower in the ongoing conflict with Russia, and is doing so with Washington’s approval.
Against this backdrop, Türkiye’s peacemaking rhetoric is starting to look increasingly unconvincing. Clearly, a mediator doesn’t have to be completely equidistant from the parties, but both sides should be able to trust it, at least on a minimum level. A mediator can’t call for a moratorium on strikes in the Black Sea while simultaneously helping one of the sides expand its weapons stockpiles; it can’t propose Istanbul as a platform for negotiations while strengthening Kiev’s military potential under the pretext of getting rid of outdated weapons.
Ankara risks overestimating Moscow’s patience
A familiar argument is being voiced by Turkish experts: Russian-Turkish relations are so deep and multifaceted, they argue, that a single deal can’t destroy them. There’s certainly some truth to that. Neither Russia nor Türkiye want to replay the scenario of the 2015 crisis. Severing ties would be detrimental to both sides.
However, Ankara is drawing an all-too-convenient conclusion that economic interdependence guarantees impunity for any foreign policy maneuver; and this is a dangerous fallacy. The Turkish leadership apparently confuses freedom of maneuver with the absence of a price to be paid for that maneuver.
Russia indeed benefits from the Turkish market, transit routes, and bilateral trade, and this is apparent to all. Türkiye remains an important economic and regional partner for Moscow. However, the dependence of the parties is not symmetrical across all sectors. In recent years, the Russian economy has demonstrated its ability to redirect raw material flows, restructure logistics, and seek new markets. Russia’s size allows it to do this quite well. For Türkiye, however, a sudden reduction in Russian energy supplies, tourism, investment, or access to the Russian market creates a more immediate and concentrated effect.
In 2025, trade between the two countries exceeded $50 billion. Russia retained a significant advantage in the trade structure: Türkiye primarily imports Russian energy resources and raw materials. That same year, it received approximately 22 billion cubic meters of gas from Russia; despite diversification, the share of Russian gas in Türkiye’s supply remained around 37%. Nearly seven million Russians visited Türkiye in 2025, securing Russia as the top source market for Türkiye’s tourism industry.
Finally, Russia is financing and constructing the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant at a cost of over $20 billion. Once operational, it is expected to supply up to 10% of Türkiye’s total electricity demand. At the end of 2025, Ankara announced an additional $9 billion in Russian financing for the project, part of which is expected to arrive in 2026–2027.
For an economy with an annual inflation rate of nearly 32% (as of July 2026), high borrowing costs, and chronic sensitivity to the price of imported energy, the loss of even a portion of these advantages will not be trivial. It will hit foreign exchange earnings, production costs, the balance of payments, and employment in tourism. The Turkish economy may not collapse overnight, but a significant reduction in ties with Russia will deprive it of several key pillars: stable energy supplies, millions of tourists, foreign exchange earnings, a market, and funding for strategic projects.
For a country already experiencing chronic inflation, pressure on the national currency, and high borrowing costs, this will mean not another temporary downturn, but the risk of a protracted systemic crisis. Ankara will not be able to maintain economic stability for long under such conditions. And this isn’t a theoretical forecast. It didn’t take long for Türkiye to feel the consequences of the 2015 crisis, provoked by Ankara after the downing of the Russian Su-24 aircraft. The crisis brought about a collapse in Russian tourist flows, restrictions on agricultural exports, and business losses, even though the economic interdependence between the two countries was significantly lower then than it is today.
Russia, for its part, is not interested in dismantling relations, but if the delivery of the weapons is confirmed, it has ample tools for selective pressure, from revising trade preferences and tourist flows to tightening the terms of energy cooperation and a tougher stance on issues in which Türkiye requires Russian assistance.
Logistics is also of particular importance. The Russian Foreign Ministry has already stated that Russian forces are striking infrastructure and ships used for delivering weapons to Kiev. If Turkish companies and transport chains are directly involved in the transfer of missiles and ammunition, Ankara will not be able to pretend that this is a purely commercial operation unrelated to Russian security.
Where is the red line?
Moscow will not react emotionally to Türkiye’s maneuver; that is not its style. A complete rupture in relations would only benefit those who have long sought to eliminate the independent Russian-Turkish communication channel and return Ankara to a disciplined, ‘Western’ line of conduct. The response must be consistent and proportionate.
Until the transfer is officially confirmed, Russia will seek a direct answer from Türkiye regarding several points: whether a final political decision has been made; on the terms and conditions of the re-export; and on the existence of any restrictions on the use of these systems to strike Russian territory. But if the weapons reach Kiev, it would no longer be possible to maintain the previous level of trust. Moscow will cease to perceive Ankara as an acceptable intermediary, will become less willing to consider Turkish interests in regional issues, and bilateral relations will become more rigid and purely pragmatic.
Russia has long assumed that Ankara is playing its own game. However, should Türkiye’s multi-vector approach turn into direct and large-scale support of the military capabilities of a state that attacks Russian territory, its civilian vessels, and critical infrastructure, this would be unacceptable for Russia. The Russian-Turkish partnership can withstand competition, mutual grievances, and even acute regional crises; but it cannot indefinitely tolerate a situation in which one side derives economic and political advantages from cooperation with Russia while simultaneously arming Russia’s adversary and posing as a mediator.
It’s time for Ankara to soberly assess the balance of risks. Russia is interested in cooperation with Türkiye but it is not irrevocably dependent on it. Moscow will find other routes, markets, and forms of regional cooperation, although such a restructuring will require time and money. For Türkiye, the Russian factor is embedded in several of its most sensitive sectors: energy, tourism, the nuclear project, trade, and regional security. Given the current state of the Turkish economy, the cost of a strategic reassessment of its own capabilities could prove significantly higher than the expected benefits of a deal with Kiev and political rapprochement with Washington.
This is precisely why the possible transfer of ATACMS missiles isn’t a matter that can be solved by another meeting between the presidents; it’s a test of the entire structure of the Russia-Türkiye relationship. If Ankara crosses the line, Russia doesn’t have to declare Türkiye an adversary – it would suffice to stop treating it as a privileged partner whose actions can always be attributed to regular political balancing.

how architecture has made space for animals across history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:35:24 UTC
05:35:24 KST

the nonhuman client was there before multispecies design
Long before architects began adding bird bricks, bee hotels and wildlife corridors to contemporary buildings, animals were already helping determine the shape of architecture. Across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, buildings were designed to accommodate pigeons, silkworms, horses, cattle and wild birds as part of systems that connected shelter, agriculture, religion, labor and power. The history of these structures suggests that the idea of multispecies architecture is a rediscovery of an older condition, as human buildings have always been influenced by nonhuman bodies.
A pigeon tower in Safavid Iran could turn the free movement of birds into agricultural fertilizer; a farmhouse in Edo-period Japan could use the heat generated by a household fire to sustain silkworm production; an Ottoman mosque might incorporate small sanctuaries for birds into its facade. Elsewhere, animal architecture expressed feudal privilege or increasingly industrial systems of extraction. Seen together, these buildings complicate the contemporary image of architecture as a purely human domain, asking, when architecture makes room for animals, who ultimately benefits from that space?
Mardavij Pigeon Tower walls | image by Գարվիք, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
pigeon towers turn animal behavior into infrastructure
Across the agricultural landscape around Isfahan, Safavid pigeon towers, or kabootar khaneh, housed large colonies of pigeons while serving a practical role in agriculture. The mudbrick structures provided protected nesting spaces, while the birds continued to fly out and forage across the surrounding landscape. Inside, rows of nesting niches filled the thick cylindrical walls. The towers protected the birds from predators and made it possible to collect their droppings, which were used as fertilizer and, in some cases, as a source of saltpeter.
The architecture was closely tied to the behavior of the pigeons. The size and arrangement of the nesting spaces, along with openings for birds to enter and ventilation through the tower, were all part of keeping the colonies healthy and productive. At the same time, the birds connected the building to the surrounding farmland, where they fed before returning to roost. The pigeons were given a protected place to nest because their presence produced something useful: fertilizer and other agricultural resources.
Shirakawa-go | image by lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
in japan, the farmhouse becomes a thermal system for silkworms
The gasshō-zukuri farmhouses of Shirakawa-gō and Gokayama are large timber houses built in the snowy mountains of central Japan, where domestic life and silkworm farming took place under the same roof. Their steep thatched roofs are perhaps their most recognizable feature, but the upper floors were also important for sericulture. Silkworms were raised in the attic spaces, while the hearth on the floor below provided heat that rose through the house.
Cooking, heating and silk production were therefore closely connected. The arrangement made the farmhouse a home and a place of production. The household relied on sericulture for income, while the layout of the building helped create the conditions needed to raise the silkworms.
Shirakawa-go | image by lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
birdhouses turn the facade into shared urban space
The Ottoman kuş evleri, or birdhouses, offer a different approach to accommodating animals in the city. Built into the walls of mosques, fountains, libraries and other public buildings across Istanbul and other Ottoman cities, these small structures provided nesting spaces for birds. Some were designed as miniature versions of the buildings they were attached to, with tiny arches, roofs, ledges and other architectural details.
Builders deliberately incorporated nesting spaces into the architecture. Unlike dovecotes built for agriculture, these birdhouses were not primarily intended to produce meat or collect manure. Their presence was connected instead to religious and charitable traditions that encouraged care for animals. The small structures brought animal life into prominent public spaces, making birds a visible part of the city.
In Ahmedabad and elsewhere in Gujarat, the chabutro offers a different way of making space for animals in the city. These elevated bird-feeding structures are found within residential neighborhoods, providing food, water and shelter for wild birds. Their raised platforms help protect the birds from predators while keeping them close to the center of daily urban life.
Carved timber and stone, shaded platforms and projecting roofs give the structures a distinct presence within the neighborhood. The chabutro is notable for placing space for birds directly within the city, making feeding and caring for birds part of the shared public environment, a tradition also connected to Jain ideas of ahiṃsā, or non-violence, and compassion toward living beings.
Ayazma Mosque birdhouse | image by R Prazeres, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
ANIMAL ARCHITECTURE AND ARISTOCRATIC POWER
The French colombier and the Grandes Écuries at the Château de Chantilly show how animal buildings could also express wealth and social status. In early modern France, dovecotes were closely tied to seigneurial power and the droit de colombier, which gave certain landowners the right to keep pigeons. Their circular walls contained rows of nesting niches, while rotating ladders allowed keepers to reach the birds. Openings connected the pigeons to the surrounding fields, where they could forage before returning to the estate. Their meat and droppings then became part of the landowner’s economy.
The colombier at the Manoir d’Ango in Normandy makes this relationship particularly visible. Its elaborate construction served the practical needs of pigeon keeping, but its scale and ornament also reflected the status of its owner. The building was part of the estate’s architecture and its system of land ownership.
At Chantilly, this relationship takes on a much larger scale. Designed by Jean Aubert between 1719 and 1735 for Louis-Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, the Grandes Écuries gave horses an architectural setting more commonly associated with palaces and monumental buildings than agricultural structures. Its vaulted interiors and extensive stone construction reflected the importance of horses to aristocratic life.
Colombier du manoir d’Ango | image by Louistisserand, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
the model farm turns animals into measurable units
By the nineteenth century, animal housing was becoming more standardized. The British Model Farm movement focused on ventilation, sanitation and making farm work more efficient. John Claudius Loudon’s writings helped establish a more systematic approach to farm buildings, with cattle, pigs and other livestock housed in spaces designed around feeding, waste removal, ventilation and productivity. This was a shift from the more integrated arrangement of earlier buildings. In the gasshō-zukuri farmhouse, domestic life and silkworm production were closely connected. Model Farms instead treated animals as things that could be measured and managed. The buildings were designed to control the conditions around the animals. Ventilation regulated the air, drainage removed waste, and feeding systems reduced the amount of labor needed to care for livestock. Materials and construction methods could also be used to control temperature. The animal was increasingly treated as part of a system of inputs and outputs: feed, heat, space and labor were calculated against the amount of meat, milk or other products produced. This approach helped establish the spatial logic of modern industrial agriculture, in which animal production became increasingly separated from everyday urban life.
Grandes Écuries, Château de Chantilly, France | P.poschadel, CC BY-SA 2.0 FR, via Wikimedia Commons
MULTISPECIES ARCHITECTURE AS A RETURN TO AN OLDER IDEA
Seen against this history, today’s interest in multispecies architecture begins to look less like a new idea and more like a return to a relationship that modern architecture has largely left behind. For centuries, animals were part of the spaces people lived and worked in, whether they were producing food and materials, contributing to household economies, protected for religious reasons, or serving as markers of wealth and status. Industrialization changed that relationship, moving animal production into increasingly controlled spaces and separating it from everyday urban life.
Looking at these buildings as animal habitats complicates the idea that multispecies architecture begins with contemporary ecological design. Some shelter birds without extracting anything from them, others depend on animals for food or agricultural production, while others turn animal housing into an expression of wealth and power. What they share is a recognition that architecture can create conditions for another species to live. The question contemporary architecture inherits is what those habitats are designed to do and what kind of relationship they establish with the animals that occupy them.
Chabutra in Ahmedabad | image by Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.

France takes aim at ultra-fast fashion with new levy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:31:52 UTC
05:31:52 KST

France takes aim at ultra-fast fashion with new levy
- France will impose a levy from Sept 1 on ultra-fast fashion items, targeting Asian e-commerce platforms like Shein with fees up to €19.50 per garment by 2030.
- The levy is based on clothing volume and repair cost, aiming to reduce environmental and economic harm caused by ultra-fast fashion.
- The measure excludes some European retailers, faces criticism and trade tension with China, but is supported by French officials and cleared by the EU Commission.
AI generated
PARIS - France will from Sept 1 impose a fee on ultra-fast fashion items that will eventually reach almost €20 (S$29) per garment, as the government targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein.
The levy follows legislation passed by the French Parliament in June to regulate so-called “ultra-fast fashion” companies, known for selling large volumes of lower quality clothing at rock-bottom prices.
It is part of a push to rein in Asian e-commerce giants including Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which have exploded in popularity in France in recent years.
“The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented,” said Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition on Aug 28 as details of the measure were published.
Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.
In 2026, companies will pay fines such as a €0.50 levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to €2 for T-shirts, €9 for jeans and €12 for a jacket.
The levy could reach up to €19.50 per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product’s pre-tax price.
A tool to collect data independently, rather than relying solely on companies’ own declarations, is under development, Lefevre’s office said.
Shein – which on Aug 31 was valued at US$26.3 billion in its long-awaited Hong Kong initial public offering – declined to comment when contacted by AFP.
Temu and AliExpress did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The measure has faced criticism over which retailers it will affect.
In July, Lefevre’s office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European and French companies.
French officials have made repeated statements that they view Shein, Temu and AliExpress as driving the surge in ultra-fast fashion.
The European Commission had also raised questions over whether the legislation complied with EU law, but Lefevre’s office said those concerns had been “dispelled” and the measure was not expected to be blocked.
China, meanwhile, warned in July of potential retaliation over the French law, slamming the regulation as “discriminatory” and in violation of trade principles.
Imports of small parcels from China into the EU have already fallen by around 30 per cent to 40 per cent since a separate €3 EU levy on such shipments came into force on July 1, according to the French government. AFP

Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes

Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes
Residents of the Kiev suburb of Milaya have accused Ukrainian officials of placing an ammunition depot dangerously close to civilian homes, according to interviews published by The Guardian on Monday.
The military storage site was hit last week during a Russian barrage. The Russian Defense Ministry said the attack targeted a warehouse complex storing components for Ukrainian long-range kamikaze drones used in strikes on logistics and e-commerce facilities in Russia.
Secondary explosions continued for hours after the strike, scattering stored military ordnance around homes just hundreds of meters from the depot, local residents told the British newspaper.
“Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” Vera, 65, reportedly said.
She and her son Sergey spent hours sheltering in a small bunker beside their home as dozens of secondary explosions rocked the area.
“I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there,” Sergey told the newspaper.
The incident killed at least 38 people and damaged more than 200 private homes and 14 apartment buildings, the Kiev military administration said on Sunday. Thirty of those killed were residents of a care home located close to the ammunition depot, according to The Guardian.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said an investigation had been launched into the “terrible negligence” that allowed munitions to be stored so close to civilians.
“Another such crime – after what happened in Vishnevoe – is absolutely unacceptable,” he wrote on X on Saturday.
A Russian strike on an ammunition depot in the Kiev suburb of Vishnevoe on July 6 also triggered massive secondary explosions, damaging hundreds of civilian buildings and causing civilian casualties. Following that incident, Zelensky and other senior Ukrainian officials vowed to prevent munitions from being stored near residential areas.
Storing ammunition near civilian housing could contravene international humanitarian law. Under Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, parties to a conflict must, “to the maximum extent feasible,” avoid locating military objectives within or near densely populated areas.

The Yaroslavl oil refinery "Yaroslavnefteorgsintez," which supplies fuel, including to the Moscow region, shut down nearly three-quarters of its capacity after a drone attack on August 28. The Moscow Times reported this, citing Reuters, writes UNN.
Details
According to two industry sources cited by Reuters, 2 of the refinery's 3 primary crude-oil processing units were damaged. The AVT-3 unit accounted for 40% of the refinery's capacity, while AVT-4 accounted for another 33%.

Several major refineries shut down in August

According to the publication, the Yaroslavl refinery has become the seventh Russian industry enterprise to partially or completely halt fuel production in August. Previously, problems arose, in particular, at refineries in the Nizhny Novgorod, Rostov, Perm, Saratov, and Volgograd regions.
According to an estimate by EA Analytics, Russia's oil-processing volumes fell in August to approximately 3.8 million barrels per day—the lowest level since 2002. Russian War Criminal Yan Petrovsky Gets 12-Year Prison Term — Previously Given Life Sentence

05:17:10 KST

The Helsinki Court of Appeals has handed down a ruling in the war crimes case involving Russian national Yan Petrovsky, also known as Vojislav Torden.
This was reported by YLE.
The court sentenced Petrovsky to 12.5 years in prison for three war crimes, although he had previously faced a life sentence.
In March of last year, the Helsinki District Court sentenced the Russian man to life in prison for four war crimes committed in 2014 during an ambush in eastern Ukraine. According to the court, the most serious of these was the murder of a Ukrainian soldier.
In the appeals court, Petrovsky demanded that the charges be dismissed or, at the very least, that his sentence be reduced. Meanwhile, the prosecutor demanded that the Russian be convicted on five counts.
The Court of Appeals concluded that Petrovsky was not liable as a leader for organizing the ambush, which was carried out on September 5, 2014, using a Ukrainian flag.
The ambush against the Aidar battalion in the Luhansk region resulted in the deaths of 22 Ukrainian soldiers and injuries to four others. The Court of Appeals determined that at least four of the deceased had sustained injuries during the attack.
The court recognized that Petrovsky served as deputy commander of the Rusich group. In addition to the commander and his deputy, at least two other members of the group participated in the ambush.
The Russian national denied his role in the group and his participation in the ambush. At the same time, the court established that Petrovsky fired a light machine gun at Ukrainian servicemen, which was classified as a war crime.
However, according to the appeals court, there was insufficient evidence in the case to prove that Petrovsky himself or the two other members of the Rusich group fired at the wounded Ukrainian servicemen.
The appellate court also determined that Petrovsky, as a leader, is not liable for the shooting at wounded Ukrainian servicemen and therefore dismissed the charges on this count.
At the same time, the court recognized that, by participating in joint military operations with others, Petrovsky bears partial responsibility for the killing and wounding of Ukrainian servicemen.
Furthermore, the court ruled that the Russian did not commit a war crime by carving the Rusich group’s symbol into the cheek of a Ukrainian serviceman.
In the court’s view, the wound was superficial, did not cause bleeding, and the damage to the cheek was temporary. Therefore, these actions “did not cause severe physical or mental suffering, which is necessary for classification as a war crime.”
The Court of Appeals also ordered Petrovsky to pay compensation to the soldiers wounded during the ambush and to the relatives of those killed.
Petrovsky was detained in August 2023.
