One dead, several missing after Grand Canyon flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:35 UTC
01:46:35 KST

One person died and about 15 people are missing or unaccounted for after a major flash flood at the Grand Canyon forced evacuations, pushed large boulders into the Colorado River and knocked out the sole water pipeline that serves tourists and residents, the US National Park Service said on Sunday.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the park service said without providing additional details. Officials from an Arizona coroner’s office were on scene.
The flooding on Saturday in Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the river, led to more than 60 people being airlifted from the depths of the canyon. The park service asked anyone with details about hikers or campers still unaccounted for to get in touch. The Arizona Department of Public Safety was helping with additional evacuations on Sunday.
Photo: AFP / J. Baird / National Park Service
The limited potable water supply because of the damaged pipeline means that starting yesterday, tourists would not be able to stay overnight at lodges and hotels within the park. Year-round residents are being asked to conserve water.
“These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources,” the park said in a statement.
Visiting the Grand Canyon can be particularly dangerous in the summer, because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon or rainy season. Clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours.
Photo: AP
Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with fellow physicians and a park ranger when heavy rain started falling on Saturday.
“We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” he said.
Later, as they made their way toward Phantom Ranch, a colleague shouted “up, up, up, up,” as a 1m debris wall headed toward them and they ran up into a patch of cacti, he said.
They were rescued by helicopter late on Saturday after making it to the Phantom Ranch area, he said.
Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and extending an existing river rapid or creating a new one. The flood was a major blow to an enduring effort to modernize the pipeline that serves 6 million visitors a year and about 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.
“Heaven help us if the whole thing down there at the bottom has to be reconstructed,” said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University. “Where are they going to get the money?”
Halting overnight stays at the park because of a lack of water is rare, although the pipeline frequently has failed over the years. A US$208 million rehabilitation of the pipeline and upgrades to the associated water delivery system started in 2023, with the park service calling it a crucial investment to ensure the park can meet the needs of residents and visitors. The project was expected to be completed next year.
Popular tourist spots, including the Bright Angel Campground, the North Kaibab Trail and Phantom Ranch, home to a historic canteen and dormitories, remained closed on Sunday. Lodging is still available just outside the park’s South Rim entrance station in Tusayan.

Silicon photonics expected to dominate AI growth, TSMC vice president says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

Silicon photonics would play a dominant role next year and make chip-level co-packaged optics (CPO) packaging possible, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) said yesterday.
“For years, critics questioned the reliability of CPO. The doubts are being thoroughly dismantled by real-world data and market validation,” TSMC vice president K.C. Hsu (徐國晉) said at a SEMI forum in Taipei.
The company is on track to enter production of CPO later this year, Hsu said in another forum arranged by Imec in Taipei yesterday, about four months after TSMC announced its progress in CPO development in May.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
Imec is the world’s leading independent research and innovation hub in nanoelectronics and digital technologies.
As server racks and data centers are expanding to handle massive artificial intelligence (AI) workloads, networks are being pushed to their limits, and that has stimulated demand for optics, the “nerve system” of data centers, Hsu said.
Last year, optical transceiver sales recorded a 25 percent growth from the previous year, with high-end products growing the fastest by 60 percent, he said.
The growth of optical transceiver sales is to accelerate this year at an annual rate of 50 percent, driven by increasing AI infrastructure expansion worldwide, Hsu said.
Next year, silicon photonics is to emerge as a dominant sales platform and on track to command more than 50 percent of the market, he said.
In 2028, AI technology upgrades would trigger a “massive new” wave of growth, he said.
To meet that demand, the underlying technology of optical transceivers is undergoing a permanent construction shift, Hsu said.
TSMC would utilize its compact universal photonic engine on a single packaged substrate, a type of CPO technology, and that would offer more than 10 times power efficiency compared with traditional copper wire-based applications, he said.
“The co-packaged optics is being adopted faster than originally expected,” Imec vice president Philippe Absil said. “I’ve seen market reports that were showing very moderate and gradual adoption, moving into 2030 when it could mean something in terms of markets.”
However, another report showed that the CPO would deliver five times the size of the traditional market today, showing that the growth is much higher than expected, he said.
“I think it’s fueled here in Taiwan,” he added.

Governor of Japan’s Kumamoto thanks Taiwan for support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

Kumamoto Prefecture Governor Takashi Kimura thanked Taiwanese for donating more than NT$300 million (US$9.47 million) to support communities affected by a magnitude 7.1 earthquake that struck the Japanese prefecture on July 28.
Kimura recorded a video message thanking people in Taiwan for their assistance, saying that Taiwanese organizations quickly launched fundraising and relief efforts after the disaster, while some groups delivered supplies and provided hot meals at evacuation shelters.
The support made local residents feel the warmth and solidarity from Taiwanese during the difficult period, he said.
Screen grab from Facebook
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs began accepting public donations for the Kumamoto earthquake relief on Aug. 1. As of Monday last week, donations from the public had exceeded NT$300 million.
Separately, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, which operates a plant in Kumamoto’s Kikuyo, donated ￥250 million (US$1.57 million) to support relief and recovery efforts.
The corporate donation is separate from the NT$300 million raised through the government-backed fundraising campaign.
In his video message, Kimura also highlighted the close travel links between Taiwan and Kumamoto.
Direct flights connect Kumamoto with four Taiwanese airports — in Taoyuan, Taichung, Tainan and Kaohsiung, he said, adding that he hoped Taiwanese visitors would return to Kumamoto and help support its recovery through tourism.
The message underscores the longstanding ties between Taiwan and Japan and the role of Taiwanese assistance in supporting Kumamoto’s recovery.
Kimura emphasized that tourism was an important part of the prefecture’s post-disaster recovery.
Kumamoto Prefecture reported that as of Friday 38 people had died and 364 had been injured, while 43,292 homes had sustained damage.
The disaster also disrupted basic infrastructure. At one point, about 108,000 households in the prefecture were without running water.
By Thursday last week, that number had fallen to about 300 as restoration work continued, local media reported.
Transportation services have also begun to recover. The Kyushu Expressway has reopened to traffic, while full operations on the affected sections of the Kyushu Shinkansen high-speed rail are expected to resume on Sept. 18, the reports said.
A month after the earthquake, Kumamoto continues to face reconstruction and relocation challenges.
Local authorities and residents are working to restore damaged infrastructure, provide housing and support evacuees, while rebuilding communities affected by the earthquake.

Taiwan codeveloped satellite wins mission award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

The cube satellite developed by the Taiwan Space Agency (TASA) in partnership with ArkEdge Space Inc and the University of Tokyo’s Intelligent Space Systems Laboratory last week won the Small Satellite Mission of the Year Award from the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA).
ONGLAISAT, an acronym for onboard globe-looking and imaging satellite, is a 6U Earth observation satellite measuring 10cm by 20cm by 30cm.
TASA developed the optical remote-sensing payload, while the Japanese side handled the satellite platform, launch arrangements and satellite operations.
Photo: CNA
The mission was to validate technologies related to the design and manufacturing of a new optical payload, as well as image processing.
The satellite was deployed from the International Space Station into low Earth orbit on Dec. 9, 2024. It conducted more than 100 imaging operations over about two months after completing initial operations last year.
The development team presented the technology and the imagery captured by ONGLAISAT at the Small Satellite Conference in the US last week, where the AIAA Small Satellite Technical Committee awarded it the Small Satellite Mission of the Year Award, TASA said.
By integrating a high-precision attitude determination and control system with an advanced optical remote-sensing system, ONGLAISAT successfully captured Earth observation imagery with a ground resolution of 2.44m, TASA said.
Using time-delay integration imaging technology, it achieved a signal-to-noise ratio of more than 100, demonstrating the potential of small, low-cost satellites to perform high-resolution optical Earth observation missions, it added.
The mission was a milestone for the commercialization of global micro-satellite constellations and high-frequency, high-resolution Earth observation, it said.
The mission proved that advanced optical and imaging-control technologies can operate even on 6U cube satellites, whereas such cutting-edge technologies previously would had to be a part of large, high-cost remote-sensing satellites, TASA said.

Official urges singer to be careful with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:30 UTC
01:46:30 KST

Yielding to political pressure in exchange for access to China’s entertainment industry rarely ends well, a Straits Exchange Foundation official said yesterday amid rumors that China is seeking to lure Taiwanese K-pop star Chou Tzu-yu (周子瑜).
Chou, who goes by Tzuyu, is the only Taiwanese member of the girl group Twice.
Her contract with JYP Entertainment is set to expire at the end of this year, and there have been widespread rumors that she would not renew it.
Screen grab from Instagram
She is reportedly planning to pursue a solo career under her parents’ agency, Yu Hai Entertainment, although China has also reportedly offered to help Tzuyu develop her career in China.
Chinese-language media have reported that China’s help would include access to broadcasting, concerts and talent agencies if she publicly endorses Beijing’s “one China” principle and says that “Taiwanese are Chinese.”
For the past decade, China has used threats and incentives to pressure Taiwanese entertainers to endorse its political positions, foundation Secretary-General Luo Wen-jia (羅文嘉) said in an interview with the Liberty Times (the sister paper of the Taipei Times).
Taiwanese artists in the Chinese market can have their work abruptly halted if they do not comply with government demands, while those who cooperate are rewarded with greater market access, Luo said.
However, those who cooperate tend to have career peaks that do not last long, he said, adding that China uses them and then discards them once they no longer have value.
China’s “united front” efforts target not only entertainers, but also politicians, influencers and media commentators, Luo said.
He criticized the legislature’s cutting of media and culture funding from the government budget, saying that lawmakers used to routinely call for more cultural funding and support for artists, regardless of which party was in power.
In a post on the paid fan platform Bubble, Chou asked her fans to wait patiently for news on her career plans and cheer her on rather than worry.
“I know there are all kinds of rumors circulating online, but even so, you’ve been willing to patiently wait for me until I can come back with new work,” she wrote.
“You don’t need to worry too much. Just cheering me on means so much to me. Your support gives me the strength to work harder and keep moving forward. I’m always so grateful to you all,” she said.
Additional reporting by Liao Li-hui

Bilingual education can learn from Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:29 UTC
01:46:29 KST

In considering what Bilingual 2030 can learn from years of classroom experience, a question deserves more attention: How can Taiwan connect the different parts of its English education ecosystem so that each strengthens the others?
Southeast Asia offers useful examples. Schools in Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam have begun partnerships with Cambridge English that deliberately connect learning materials, student assessment and teacher development. The principle is straightforward: What students learn, how their progress is measured and how teachers develop professionally should reinforce one another.
Much of this infrastructure already exists in Taiwan. Cambridge English materials and qualifications have a presence here, while the Ministry of Education has invested substantially in preparing and supporting teachers through Bilingual 2030. Universities, schools and educational organizations have developed additional professional-development programs of their own.
The regional developments therefore raise a useful question: Could Taiwan connect these strengths even more closely?
One possibility worth exploring is the teacher-development part of the Cambridge English ecosystem. Cambridge’s teacher-development pathways include qualifications such as Teaching Knowledge Test (TKT), Certificate in English Language Teaching to Adults (CELTA) and the Diploma in English Language Teaching to Adults (DELTA). They serve educators at different stages of professional development, but together they show that international frameworks can support not only the assessment of student achievement, but the continuing development of the teachers helping students reach those standards.
Taiwan already has encouraging experience in this area.
A 2022 study by researchers at National Taipei University of Technology followed 50 primary and secondary teachers in Taiwan through eight weeks of TKT-focused professional development. The researchers found improvements in teachers’ understanding of teaching theory and methodology, alongside greater diversity in teaching materials and more varied approaches to lesson planning, classroom activities and student interaction.
Teacher development can complete that cycle by giving educators additional knowledge, techniques and professional perspectives with which to respond.
Learning, assessment and teacher development then reinforce one another: Classroom experiences produce learning; assessment provides evidence of that learning; professional development helps teachers interpret and respond to what the evidence reveals; and what teachers learn feeds back into the classroom.
This is what makes the Southeast Asian partnerships worth watching from Taiwan. It is less about any particular program than the principle of connecting educational resources so that each strengthens the others.
Taiwan is well positioned to deepen those connections. Years of Bilingual 2030 implementation have generated valuable classroom experience, substantial investment has expanded teacher development, and the nation can draw on locally developed expertise and international professional-development frameworks.
As Bilingual 2030 evolves, Taiwan can continue building on what has already been accomplished while remaining open to useful ideas emerging elsewhere in the region. Connecting learning, assessment and teacher development more closely could help ensure that investment in each ultimately reaches the place where it matters most: the learning experiences of Taiwan’s students.
Daniel Eyrich is director of English Studies at CenYing English in Keelung and has more than 15 years of experience in English language teaching, assessment and teacher development in Taiwan.

Taiwan, US to boost workforce efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:29 UTC
01:46:29 KST

American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) Director Raymond Greene yesterday announced new measures to bolster bilateral cooperation on semiconductor workforce development, saying at an event in Taipei that the measures would expand educational pathways to cultivate talent in both countries.
“In doing so, we will not only deliver high-quality jobs for US and Taiwan workers in critical sectors, but we will also grow and strengthen our enduring partnership,” Greene said in his opening remarks at the Freedom 250 Workforce First Summit.
The summit — cohosted by AIT, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Industrial Development Administration — brought together 150 government, industry and academic leaders from Taiwan and the US to enhance bilateral cooperation on workforce development.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Two measures aim to encourage more US students to study in Taiwan in high-tech fields, Greene said.
One of the measures is a US$20 million commitment from the Garcia Family Foundation to the University of Arizona to support students pursuing study-abroad opportunities, potentially also in Taiwan, he said.
The other initiative would bring two additional graduate students to National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University next year under the Fulbright Semiconductor Scholarship, he said.
“These actions and programs serve as a powerful catalyst, a source of inspiration for other institutions here today to develop their own institutional and financial incentives and academic pathways to ensure today’s rising talents become the next generation of leaders in critical institutions,” Greene said.
It is part of the deepening cooperation between Taiwan and the US in high-tech sectors, with both sides developing and expanding educational pathways to cultivate talent and align their workforce preparation efforts, he said.
Also speaking at the event, Minister of Education Cheng Ying-yao (鄭英耀) said that US students would be able to learn directly from Taiwanese educators, researchers, engineers, industry experts and other students.
“Yet, this is not one-way learning,” Cheng said. “US students will experience Taiwan’s semiconductor ecosystem firsthand, while Taiwanese students gain international perspectives by learning alongside their US peers.”
During the summit, Cheng and Greene also witnessed the signing of a memorandum of intent between the Foundation for International Cooperation in Higher Education of Taiwan and the US-based SEMI Foundation to promote closer cooperation between the two organizations.
The Taipei-based foundation promotes international cooperation in Taiwan’s higher education sector, while the SEMI Foundation, the nonprofit arm of microelectronics industry association SEMI, focuses on improving the global semiconductor talent pipeline through workforce development programs.

====================================================================================================

Is your brain rotted enough for microdramas?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:27 UTC
01:46:27 KST

If an alien species learned about humanity solely through microdramas, they would conclude that our lives revolve around spicy secret affairs, billionaire suitors and the occasional werewolf or vampire. There is a reason I have avoided writing about them until now.
These sub-two-minute soaps deliver serialized hits of dopamine that keep viewers watching — or get them to pay — via the classic cliffhanger. It is television production optimized for the smartphone and attention economy.
They went mainstream in China, where they are known as duanju (短劇), during the COVID-19 pandemic and overtook domestic box office revenue last year. Now they are coming for the world, as much as I wish they were not.
Overseas revenue is estimated to reach US$3.6 billion this year and US$9.5 billion by 2031, analytics firm Media Partners Asia said.
Downloads of short drama apps globally surpassed 850 million in the first quarter of this year, up 140 percent from the previous 12 months, separate data from Sensor Tower showed.
That growth is happening even in the absence of any good content (I have yet to see one I could recommend). Imagine what a breakout hit could do.
No wonder Hollywood wants in, with major studios from Fox Entertainment to Walt Disney Co reportedly exploring the format. Yet simply throwing money and star power at the emerging medium could actually put it at disadvantage to China’s growing dominance over the sector.
It is impossible to discuss this trend without mentioning the rise and fall of Quibi. Originally a portmanteau for “quick bites,” its name has since become shorthand for a high-profile, expensive failure in the tech and entertainment industries. The platform raised US$1.8 billion to bring Hollywood-grade production to vertical video before shuttering less than a year after its launch in 2020.
Many still cite Quibi as evidence that the microdrama trend would not last. Others have blamed the timing of its launch, coinciding with the pandemic, for its failure — an odd defense given the lockdowns helped the format take off in China.
The real lesson is that you do not need multimillion-dollar budgets for something viewers watch while scrolling at the dentist’s office, in the bathroom or, increasingly, while waiting for an artificial intelligence (AI) tool to respond.
Quibi began too-big-not-to-fail. China’s challengers reversed the model, growing audiences with modest budgets and no stars, echoing the way the creator economy was built on TikTok and Alphabet Inc’s YouTube.
Globally, most of the market share has coalesced around five Chinese-origin players you have probably never heard of — ReelShort, DramaBox, DramaWave, NetShort and GoodShort — with 300 smaller apps behind them, Media Partners Asia said.
Like with many tech-adjacent industries in China, brutal competition has led to rapid iteration. Domestic microdrama producers essentially use a “spray and pray” method, churning out 3,000 new productions a month, according to a Peking University report.
It seems to be working. Users spend about two hours a day on them, a trade group said last year. Average daily time spent internationally hit 25 minutes in April, up 85 percent from January last year, Sensor Tower said. Traditional streaming services remained broadly flat at about 35 minutes.
AI is emerging as the sector’s other secret weapon. While there has been a lot of trepidation about its rise in Hollywood, microdrama studios have embraced the technology for everything from subtitling, script-writing and, increasingly, creating entire shows. As Western labs shifted resources to coding, Chinese AI video generators continue to dominate global benchmarks.
The Peking University researchers estimated that the industry supported more than 2 million jobs last year. That combination of heavy AI adoption and rapid job creation makes the nascent sector the ultimate real-time case study for whether the technology would democratize creativity and expand employment (as its proponents say) or hollow it out (what is likely to happen in the near term).
However, Sora, OpenAI’s short-lived AI video platform-cum-TikTok clone might offer another warning. Quibi might have spent too much on production, but Sora went in the opposite direction. It let users generate pure brainrot, often lacking even the pretense of a storyline.
Microdrama producers relying entirely on AI would find audiences are already sick of slop. AI is better used as a tool than a substitute for storytellers.
China’s approach carries risks. Becoming too big could put a TikTok-like target on these apps. Many have flown under the regulatory radar so far. (How much harm can binging on Duke With Benefits really do?) That could change if policymakers view this latest soft power lever as a threat.
Then there is looming labor uncertainties for the US, as many of these productions employ nonunion workers.
It is easy to dismiss this trend as too mind-numbing to last, but many — myself included — initially felt the same about the lip-syncing videos in TikTok’s early days. Eventually, US tech firms were forced to copy the playbook in the form of YouTube Shorts and Meta Platforms Inc’s Instagram Reels.
For better or worse, microdramas can no longer be dismissed as a passing fad. The only thing shrinking faster than our attention spans might be the US’ window to compete.
Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Punjab groundwater crisis shows signs of reversal, AAP cites rise in canal-water use

General Secretary and Media In-Charge, 'AAP' Punjab
NEW DELHI: Punjab’s groundwater crisis is showing signs of improvement, with the latest assessment indicating a decline in groundwater extraction and an increase in canal-water utilisation, AAP Punjab media in-charge Baltej Pannu said on Monday.Addressing a press conference in Chandigarh earlier today, Pannu attributed the improvement to the Bhagwant Mann government’s efforts to strengthen canal infrastructure, increase the use of canal water and reduce dependence on groundwater.Pannu said canal-water utilisation has risen to around 80-82% from roughly 21% in 2022. He said the government had activated 14,100 watercourses, restored more than 400 km of defunct canals and concretised over 1,000 km of canals. Recharge points have also been developed along repaired canal infrastructure, he said.
According to Pannu, Punjab’s stage of groundwater extraction declined from 163.80% in 2021-22 to 156.36% in 2025 and 152.22% in 2025-26. Annual groundwater extraction also fell from around 28.01 billion cubic metres to 26.32 billion cubic metres.
95 dark-zone blocks show improvementPannu said the latest assessment showed improvement in 95 of Punjab’s 153 dark-zone blocks, while the number of critical blocks fell from 10 to six.
Four blocks — Arniwala in Fazilka, Makhu in Ferozepur, Hajipur in Hoshiarpur and Narot Jaimal Singh in Pathankot — have moved into the safe category, he said.Another 14 blocks have recorded significant improvement, according to Pannu.Pannu said total annual groundwater recharge has increased to 19.14 billion cubic metres, including 5.53 billion cubic metres from rainfall and 5.5 billion cubic metres through canal water. Canal-water recharge increased from 4.5 billion cubic metres last year to 5.5 billion cubic metres this year, he said.

Kalshi permanently bans former GOP Rep. George Santos over illegal trading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:44:14 UTC
01:44:14 KST

The prediction market platform Kalshi announced on Monday it has permanently banned former Republican Rep. George Santos and fined him $71,356 for allegedly using the app to trade on his own attendance at this year's State of the Union address.
It's the first ban of its kind on the platform, the company confirmed on Monday.
In the weeks leading up to President Donald Trump's speech in February, Santos, who represented New York's 3rd Congressional District from January 2023 until his expulsion from Congress later that same year, allegedly made more than $17,000 by betting on whether he would attend.
In the weeks leading up to the event, Santos "began making a series of public statements regarding his attendance at the event in an attempt to influence the price of Yes and No contracts, respectively. Some of these included false or misleading statements," according to a Kalshi announcement of the disciplinary action, released Monday. Those actions violated the company's rules on trading on non-public information, Kalshi said.
In one X post from days before Trump's address, Santos said: "I'm going to be there for the State of Union in the gallery, guys." On the day of the State of the Union, Santos posted he was watching from the airport.
Santos shot back at Kalshi on Monday in a post to X.
"Hey @Kalshi thanks for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform. Let's see how much longer you guys are around for," the former lawmaker wrote, ending the post with a "kiss mark" emoji.
Kalshi's disciplinary action is not the first time Santos has drawn fire for the incident.
After Kalshi detected his trades and referred him to federal investigators, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in July ordered Santos to pay $35,000 for trading on State of the Union attendance. The federal regulator also banned Santos from trading for three years. Santos at the time shared a statement from his lawyer saying he had settled without admitting to any of the CFTC's findings.
In June, amid the federal investigation, Polymarket, a rival prediction market platform, ended its paid relationship with Santos, who had been working as an online influencer for the company.
Before Santos was sworn into office in 2023, doubts about his biography had emerged. His time in Congress was punctuated by a House Ethics Committee investigation that found "substantial evidence of wrongdoing." He became the first member of the House to be expelled in more than 20 years.
Santos had also been sentenced to 87 months in prison for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, though President Donald Trump commuted his sentence last fall.
Kalshi also announced settlements on Monday with three political candidates who traded on contracts related to their candidacies: a governor candidate in California, another gubernatorial hopeful in Maine, and a congressional candidate in North Carolina. All have to pay penalties and are banned from Kalshi for three years, but the company said all three complied with the investigations, unlike Santos.
While the candidates for California and Maine governor lost their races, Laurie Buckhout is the Republican nominee for the battleground North Carolina 1st Congressional District, where she faces Democratic incumbent Rep. Don Davis. Buckhout will have to pay a penalty of just under $2,600 for her trades.
"I bet on myself. Literally," Buckhout said in a statement. "It was a dumb mistake, and as soon as I learned there was an issue, I worked to make it right. Safe to say my career as a Kalshi trader was short-lived."
— CNBC's Davis Giangiulio contributed reporting
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

How to Stop Wasting So Much Food in Your Kid’s Lunchbox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:20:05 UTC
01:20:05 KST

Collect everything the average American kid throws away in the school cafeteria over a single year, pile it on a scale, and you'd be looking at roughly 39 lbs of food. That’s about what a typical 4-year-old weighs.
Multiply that across the country, and school food waste adds up to an estimated 530,000 tons every year—an alarming amount of uneaten sandwiches, rejected fruit, and unopened snacks.
That makes food waste difficult to dismiss as somebody else’s problem. “If you eat food, you’re part of this whether you like it or not,” says Lauren Click, founder of the nonprofit Let’s Go Compost, which runs food-waste programming in more than 600 schools, libraries, and community centers. The flip side is that you’re also in a position to waste less—starting with a packed lunch, one of the few pieces of the food system a family fully controls.
Here’s how experts recommend packing a school lunch that produces less trash—and stands a better chance of getting eaten.
See what comes home
Before you overhaul your lunch-packing routine, spend a couple weeks paying attention to what returns at the end of the day. Which foods are untouched? Is the bologna sandwich always missing exactly one bite? What never even made it out of the wrapper?
After a few days, you’ll probably start to notice a pattern. “If you pack based on what actually comes home, not what seems balanced on paper, you can track it each week and adjust over time,” says Lizzie Horvitz, founder and CEO of Finch, a platform that evaluates products for sustainability.
You don’t have to keep tabs on the lunchbox all year. August and September are when parents are still figuring out what—and how much—their kids will eat. “If you're really paying attention to ‘what's my kid eating?’ and ‘what's my kid consistently bringing home?’” Horvitz says, “there really shouldn't be any waste after a couple of weeks.”
Ask your kid what happened
Seeing what comes home is only half the job. You also need to find out why—and good luck guessing correctly.
Click has heard every version of this story: A kid suddenly stops eating apples, and their parent assumes they don’t like the fruit. The real problem? A classmate declared apples uncool. “You can't make assumptions, because you'll never guess what's going on in the mind of a 5-year-old,” she says.
Keep the conversation curious, not accusatory. Ask your kid who they sit with, how much time they have to eat, and what their friends bring. Maybe the orange takes too long to peel, or they can’t open one of the containers without help. Maybe their friend brings two sandwiches and shares one every day—in which case, congratulations, you can stop making a sandwich.
Save new foods for dinner
The school cafeteria isn't exactly an ideal tasting room. Lunch periods are short, cafeterias can be loud and chaotic, and no one is sitting nearby encouraging your kid to give that unfamiliar vegetable one more chance. (Rutabaga, anyone?)
“Maybe this isn't the time to have a really balanced, try-new-things meal,” Horvitz says. “Let's save that for meals at home.” That's not an argument for packing nothing but cookies. It means lunch should mostly consist of foods you already know your child will eat; save the experiments for dinner, when you’re there to encourage them.
Choose the food before the lunchbox
Compartmentalized bento boxes are adorable. They're also built for a very specific amount (and shape) of food, which may not match what—or how much—your kid eats.
Lindsey Schoenfeld, a registered dietitian nutritionist, chef, and co-author of To Your Taste: How to Eat Well and Feel Better for Your Whole Life, suggests starting with the food instead. Ask your kid what they ate all summer and which lunches they loved last year. Then choose containers that fit those foods. The folded half-sandwich that nestled perfectly into one tiny compartment in second grade might not cut it for a middle-schooler.
Before splurging on new gear, check your cabinets. “There's so many containers that we have around the house,” Schoenfeld says. “Maybe they don't have a lid right now. Maybe we need to dig through a few shelves.” You might need a new lunchbox, but you probably don't need every container inside it to be new too.
Reusable containers only reduce waste if you use them over and over, so make cleanup as painless as possible. Many silicone bags and food containers can go straight into the dishwasher—check the manufacturer’s instructions—and you don’t need to scrub them spotless first. “The dishwasher’s job is to make them completely spotless,” Horvitz says.
Pack the amount your child actually eats
An oversized container practically begs to be filled, Schoenfeld says—and parents often respond by packing more than their kid will eat.
As a rough starting point, she suggests about half a cup of fruit, or one small piece of whole fruit, for younger elementary-school kids, in addition to a quarter- to half-cup of vegetables and one serving of grains, such as a slice of bread or a 6-inch tortilla. Middle-schoolers might need the higher end of those ranges, while high-schoolers may eat a full cup of produce and two servings of grains.
But kids aren’t measuring cups. “They grow at different times, and their activity is very different,” Schoenfeld says. One child might spend all day running around on the playground or practicing with the marching band, while another might take medication that suppresses their appetite at lunchtime. If the same amount keeps returning, try sending less before deciding your child has rejected the food altogether.
Find out what time lunch starts
Plenty of parents don’t know what time their kid eats lunch. It's worth checking: Because schools stagger lunch by grade, some are sitting down with their sandwiches at 10:30 a.m.
That can explain a lot. A child who ate breakfast at 7 might not be hungry three and a half hours later, even though they're ravenous when they get home. Pack a little less for an early lunch, Schoenfeld suggests, and have a substantial snack ready after school. She likes options that include a real food group, such as cheese and whole-grain crackers, fruit, or carrot sticks.
“It's good to capture these kids when they're hungry and you have something good ready,” she says.
Send last night's dinner
One of the easiest ways to waste less is to pack food you already made—and already know your child likes.
Jessica Randhawa, the chef and recipe developer behind The Forked Spoon, has used vacuum-insulated stainless-steel containers for her son's lunch since preschool. In the morning, she reheats leftovers—vegetables, meat, whatever is in the fridge—and transfers them to the insulated container. In winter, she sends leftover chicken soup, one of his favorites, in a larger container with a handle. A reusable metal spork goes in with it.
Her larger point: The container matters far less than whether the food gets eaten. “The best low-waste lunch system is one that the child actually eats,” Randhawa says. “Reusable containers aren’t helpful if the food inside is repeatedly wasted.”
Open the lunchbox before the pantry
When a hungry kid walks through the door, take a look inside their lunchbox before handing over a new snack. Schoenfeld does this automatically. “I’m known for saying, ‘Oh, you’re hungry?’” Schoenfeld says. “I just open the lunchbox back up. ‘Look, it’s perfect. It’s ready to go.’”
Of course, food safety gets the final say. Shelf-stable foods—crackers, a sealed pouch, an unopened bag of chips—can go back into the pantry or be eaten later. Perishable food is a different story: If it didn’t stay cold during the school day, toss it.
Don't automatically rule out single-serve packages
An individually packaged snack isn’t always an environmental villain. If your kid brings home an unopened package of crackers, it can go straight back into the pantry. “It’s like it never came to school,” Horvitz says.
Loose crackers can be saved too, of course, but people are often more willing to toss food that’s already been opened and portioned out. Buying in bulk and using reusable containers still produces the least packaging—but a single-serve snack that gets eaten another day can be better than food that lands in the trash.
“If we're assuming a kid is eating everything in their lunchbox, we of course want to stray from individually packaged food,” Horvitz says. But if your child is unpredictable about what they'll eat, a sealed package that comes home isn't necessarily a failure. The best option is to buy in bulk and portion food into reusable containers; after that, a packaged snack that gets eaten another day can be better than loose food that lands in the trash.
The same general rule applies to drinks: A reusable bottle is best, and pouring juice from a large jug creates less packaging than sending an individual box. If you do pack a can, don't crush it afterward; Horvitz notes that intact cans are easier for recycling facilities to sort.
Consider a secondhand lunchbox
There's no rule that says a lunchbox has to be new. Click suggests checking Facebook Marketplace, Poshmark, and eBay, where last year's enthusiasm for a particular cartoon character is now available at a discount. “They have every character you can think of,” she says.
Just don't try to replace every disposable item in one frantic back-to-school shopping trip. Pick one change, get used to it, and then consider another. “Don't try to go zero-waste in one day, because you're gonna get frustrated,” Click says. “It's like saying you're gonna lose 50 lbs in one month.”
Be skeptical of “compostable” packaging
“Compostable” packaging usually needs more than a trash can—or even a backyard compost pile. Many products break down only in commercial composting facilities. Yet a 2025 national analysis found that just 18.1% of the sampled U.S. population had access to a curbside or drop-off program that accepted food scraps and at least some forms of compostable packaging. If your local program doesn’t accept these products, they’ll probably end up in a landfill.
“The word compostable doesn't mean it will compost,” Click says. She recommends choosing reusable items first. If you do buy compostable products, make sure you have a realistic way to compost them—either at home, if they’re certified for home composting, or through a local service that accepts and processes them.
Show kids where the trash goes
The most effective tool for cutting lunch waste isn't a product. It might be a field trip.
Click takes children to landfills, where the hard hats, safety vests, and enormous trucks are a hit. But the adults tend to leave with the bigger revelation. “You start to see the birds there eating trash,” she says. “You're really faced with this reality of, like, you contribute to this.”
Many recycling facilities offer free tours, and county extension offices around the country run gardening and composting programs for kids. The point isn’t to make children feel guilty about every granola-bar wrapper. It’s to help them see where their trash ends up—and why small changes matter.
“There's not a magical product that you can order online and have it shipped with two-day shipping that will solve this,” Click says. “It really comes down to healthy daily habits that you build over time.”

4 Easy Ways to Start the Mediterranean Diet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:16:07 UTC
01:16:07 KST

The Mediterranean diet is one of the most researched and most prescribed eating plans for weight loss, heart health, and many conditions in between. Research has linked it to better health outcomes, including lower rates of Type 2 diabetes, stroke, heart issues, cancer, and even better cognitive health.
Yet many people still have misconceptions about the Mediterranean diet: mainly that it’s expensive and difficult. “I think that people just have to be told that it is affordable and it's quite easy,” says Joan Salge Blake, clinical professor of nutrition at Boston University, author of the book Nutrition & You, and the host of the nutrition podcast Spot On!
The pillars of the Mediterranean diet include eating more vegetables, whole grains, fish, and olive oil, and consuming minimal amounts of alcohol, red meat, and saturated fats. Getting good amounts of physical and social activity is a core tenet of the lifestyle plan, too. But you don’t have to overhaul your diet overnight. “Try to take one one or two small steps at a time, and you'll eventually get there,” says Angel Planells, a registered dietitian in Seattle and spokesperson for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.
We spoke to experts about easy ways to start adopting the Mediterranean diet.
Embrace frozen and canned produce
Americans are woefully behind on their produce intake. Only about 12% of U.S. adults ate the recommended amount of fruit, and 10% ate enough vegetables, according to the latest analysis by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention..
A great way to start getting more produce on your plate is through your freezer and pantry, Blake says. When you’re first learning to prepare fresh fruits and vegetables, they can become expensive—especially if they end up rotting away, forgotten, in a fridge drawer. Since grocery bills have skyrocketed over the last few years, that can make the shift even more daunting. But Blake points out that frozen and canned produce can carry the same nutrients in an easier-to-store, more cost-effective format.
“Some people think, ‘Oh, I’ve got to cook from scratch, and everything's got to be fresh,’” says Blake. “And the answer is, ‘No, it does not.’”
It’s also easier to deal with. “Canned and frozen produce is cleaned, chopped, and ready to go. It's like having Rachael Ray in your freezer and pantry,” she says. “Fresh is not always best.”
Choose frozen or canned seafood
Fresh seafood is also often pricey, but it’s not a requirement that your seafood be fresh, either.
“It could be frozen. It could be out of a can,” Blake says. Tuna and salmon also come packaged in a pouch, which is “extremely, extremely affordable and really, really good for you based on the science that we have today,” she says.
For time-strapped Americans, frozen and canned foods can help speed things along, reduce food waste, and ensure that there’s always some kind of produce at the ready.
“These are as nutritious as fresh, and they're convenient, and this way you don't have to go back to the supermarket more than once a week,” she says. She also recommends checking out your local supermarket’s deals to see what’s on sale that week.
Diversify your protein sources
“We get kind of fixated that it has to be animal protein, and that's clearly not the case,” says Planells. For animal protein, the Mediterranean diet favors seafood and leaner cuts of meat, and it also recommends plant-based sources of protein like beans and lentils.
Despite rising grocery costs, a May 2026 report from the American Farm Bureau Federation finds that “America’s demand for meat continues to grow.” As of July, ground beef prices were up 10% from the same time in 2025.
“Everyone wants protein, protein, protein, but we're going to go broke,” says Planells.
Swap in leaner cuts and types of meat, embrace eggs, and try more plant-based protein like tofu, beans, nuts, and seeds, he recommends, which both comply with the Mediterranean diet and might end up being a cost effective and healthier trade.
You can also add leaner, greener proteins into meaty dishes you already like. “If you're going to make a chili, what you can do instead of putting in like 2 lbs of ground beef is put in 1 lb of lean ground beef and double up or triple up on beans,” Blake suggests. “You cut the cost of that meal per serving, and you also decrease the saturated fat and increase the fiber per serving.”
Take baby steps
“Whatever way people eat, whatever way they shop, it would be better to try to look into their life and try to make small, gradual changes in what they're doing than trying to give them the pathway to excellence,” says Planells. Instead of fried foods, opt for baked, grilled, or steamed. In terms of meats, pick leaner cuts. Choose healthier snacks, like nuts or yogurt, instead of products like chips. Swap in whole grains like quinoa, brown rice, and whole wheat pasta instead of processed versions.
“Every time we have a meal or snack, it's an opportunity to try to make it as nutrient-rich as possible,” says Planells.
When Planells works with a patient, he often suggests making one small diet-related and physical-related change a week.
Movement is just as key to the Mediterranean lifestyle as the food is. When researchers originally started studying the diets and lifestyles of people in the region, Blake says, they found that physical activity was an important part. “We really need to start getting movement in our life as a habit,” says Blake.
Correction, Aug. 31
The original version of this story misspelled a dietitian's name; she is Joan Salge Blake, not Joan Saldge Blake.

BUDAPEST, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Hungary has completed the legislative and institutional measures required to unlock around 10 billion euros (about 11.6 billion U.S. dollars) in previously frozen funds from the European Union's (EU) Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), Transportation and Investment Minister David Vitezy said on Monday.
Speaking at a press conference in Budapest, Vitezy said the government had met all the milestones and "super milestones" agreed with the European Commission following a political agreement reached in May between Prime Minister Peter Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
According to the minister, more than 100 pieces of legislation were adopted during the process, alongside the establishment of new institutions and the launch or completion of several projects. He said much of the legislative work concerned anti-corruption measures required for access to the funds.
"The prime minister tasked me with making sure that we leave not a single euro cent behind and bring home all the available funds. I can report that we succeeded," Vitezy said.
He added that the government now intends to use the funds primarily for railway modernization, affordable housing and student accommodation, water-management projects aimed at mitigating increasingly frequent droughts, and investments in renewable energy and the electricity grid.
Significant portions of EU funding for Hungary were frozen under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban's government over EU concerns about corruption, public procurement and rule-of-law issues.
The Magyar government made restoring access to frozen EU funds one of its priorities after taking office earlier this year, and has introduced a series of institutional and legislative changes aimed at meeting the European Commission's conditions. ■

Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with Mongolian President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Summit 2026 in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Aug. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Yan Yan)
BISHKEK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Monday that China is ready to work with Mongolia to foster more areas of growth for mutually beneficial cooperation and advance hand in hand along the respective paths of modernization.
Xi made the remarks in a meeting with Mongolian President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Summit 2026 in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
Noting that China and Mongolia are close neighbors connected by mountains and rivers, Xi said that peaceful coexistence, mutual support and solidarity as well as mutually beneficial cooperation have always been the mainstream and defining feature of bilateral relations.
China will continue to place China-Mongolia relations in an important position in its neighborhood diplomacy, and work together with Mongolia to consolidate strategic mutual trust, deepen mutually beneficial cooperation and promote people-to-people connectivity, so as to inject greater vitality into the comprehensive strategic partnership and promote the building of the China-Mongolia community with a shared future, Xi said.
Both sides should consolidate the political foundation for the development of China-Mongolia relations, respect each other's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, and respect each other's core interests and major concerns, Xi said.
Xi voiced China's readiness to strengthen alignment of development strategies with Mongolia, promote traditional cooperation in trade, connectivity as well as energy and mineral resources, and explore the potential for cooperation in emerging fields such as green minerals, artificial intelligence and the digital economy.
China hopes that Mongolia will effectively protect the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises, said Xi, urging both sides to strengthen coordination and cooperation in multilateral affairs and jointly address global challenges.
Khurelsukh, for his part, said that Mongolia and China are friendly neighbors who have always respected and trusted each other and maintained good-neighborly relations, regardless of changes in the international situation.
China's development has provided major opportunities for neighboring countries and is driving the development of Asia and the world, he added.
Deepening friendly cooperation with China is a top priority of Mongolia's foreign policy, he said, adding that Mongolia stands ready to continuously consolidate political mutual trust with China, enhance cooperation in trade and investment, industry, agriculture, mining and the green economy, and advance bilateral relations to new heights.
Mongolia firmly adheres to the one-China principle and recognizes that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory, while issues related to Xinjiang, Xizang and Hong Kong are China's internal affairs, he said.
The four major global initiatives proposed by Xi and the vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity are of great significance for maintaining world peace and security, promoting sustainable development and addressing global challenges, he said, adding that Mongolia stands ready to work with China to jointly implement them. ■

Infant feeding practices may influence the timing of puberty in girls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:00:23 UTC
01:00:23 KST

A large study published in The Journal of Nutrition found that girls who consumed human breast milk as infants tended to start puberty slightly later than those fed exclusively with infant formula. The research suggests that early feeding practices might influence the timeline of sexual development in females, though the same pattern was not observed in boys.
Puberty is the transitional phase of physical maturation when a child develops into an adult. Over recent decades, medical professionals globally have noted a general trend of puberty starting at younger ages, particularly in girls. Early puberty is a public health concern because it is associated with a higher risk of various adult health issues, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and certain reproductive cancers.
Human sexual development is shaped by many elements, including genetics, childhood body weight, and socioeconomic status. Medical researchers have also questioned whether an infant’s first foods might play a role in this biological clock. Human milk provides infants with unique hormones and nutritional components that infant formula lacks, prompting investigations into its long-term effects on physical growth.
The current study was led by Marta Pinto da Costa, a researcher at the Institute of Public Health of the University of Porto in Portugal, alongside several colleagues. The team wanted to know if consuming human milk, as well as the duration and exclusivity of that feeding, was associated with the timing of puberty. They noted that previous studies on this topic had yielded conflicting results, with some finding a protective effect against early puberty and others finding no link at all.
To investigate this question, the researchers examined data from a large birth cohort study called Generation XXI. This project enrolled expectant mothers at public maternity hospitals in Porto, Portugal, between 2005 and 2006. The researchers tracked a final sample of 4,745 children from birth through adolescence.
Parents were interviewed about their infant feeding practices at multiple points when the children were six, 15, and 24 months old, and again at four years old. The researchers categorized the children into four groups based on their diets. These groups included children who never received human milk, those who received human milk along with formula or other foods, those exclusively fed human milk for less than four months, and those exclusively fed human milk for four months or longer.
The four-month cutoff was chosen because Portugal provides four months of fully paid maternity leave, heavily influencing infant feeding timelines in the region. When the children reached 10 years of age, trained nurses evaluated their physical development. The nurses looked for established markers of puberty, such as breast growth and pubic hair in girls, and genital growth and pubic hair in boys.
These characteristics were graded on a standard medical scale known as Tanner stages, which ranges from one (prepubertal) to five (fully mature). To improve the accuracy of their assessments, the researchers combined the individual Tanner stages into a total puberty score ranging from two to 10. A score of three or higher indicated that a child had officially started puberty. Later, at ages 13 and 18, female participants also reported the age at which they experienced menarche, their first menstrual cycle.
The research team used statistical models to compare the early feeding categories with the puberty scores at age 10 and the age of the first menstrual cycle. They adjusted their calculations to account for other factors that might sway the results. These adjusted variables included the mother’s age and education, the mother’s own age at her first period, and the child’s birth weight.
The researchers found that girls who received human milk had a lower likelihood of showing advanced puberty scores at age 10 compared to girls who were never fed human milk. This pattern was most pronounced among girls who were exclusively fed human milk for at least four months. Essentially, any exposure to human milk in infancy was associated with a less advanced stage of puberty by age 10.
The initial analysis also indicated that exclusive human milk feeding was linked with a later onset of the first menstrual cycle in girls. However, this specific link was no longer statistically significant once the researchers factored in the children’s body mass index at age 10. Body mass index is a common medical tool that estimates body fat based on height and weight. This attenuation suggests that childhood body weight might partly mediate the relationship between early feeding and the timing of menstruation.
Previous research indicates that longer durations of breastfeeding often protect against childhood obesity, a condition frequently linked to earlier puberty onset. Human milk contains hormones like leptin, which helps regulate infant appetite and acts as a chemical signal communicating the body’s nutritional status to the brain. While leptin is known to influence the biological pathways that trigger reproductive maturity, researchers note that the exact way leptin from breast milk might shape a child’s long-term hormone levels remains speculative. Still, breast milk could indirectly delay puberty by preventing rapid weight gain in early childhood.
In boys, the researchers did not find consistent statistical associations between human milk feeding and puberty scores. One specific group of boys, those who received some human milk but were never exclusively fed it, showed a lower likelihood of having the highest puberty scores. The researchers noted that this finding was based on a very small number of boys who had reached advanced puberty by age 10, meaning the result is less reliable. Overall, boys tend to enter puberty later than girls, which makes early signs of maturation much harder to detect at age 10.
The study relies on observational data, meaning it cannot prove that human milk directly causes a delay in puberty. Other unmeasured lifestyle variables associated with families who breastfeed might contribute to the observed timeline. For instance, mothers with more education tend to breastfeed longer, and they might also foster habits that influence child health, such as consistent sleep routines and higher diet quality.
Additionally, infant feeding details were reported by parents months or years after the fact, which introduces the possibility of memory errors. Measuring the exact stages of puberty, particularly in boys, also involves some subjective judgment by the examining nurses.
Future studies could track actual hormone levels to see if compounds found in human milk interact with a child’s endocrine system over time. Researchers may also need to evaluate boys at older ages to capture a more complete picture of their maturation timeline.
The study, “Human Milk Feeding Practices and Pubertal Timing: Insights from the Generation XXI Population-Based Birth Cohort,” was authored by Marta Pinto da Costa, Milton Severo, Carla Lopes, Augusto Anguita-Ruiz, Joana Araújo, and Sofia Vilela.

double-helix stairs frame wetland views inside xiang architects’ wuhan observation tower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:55:05 UTC
00:55:05 KST

Xiang Architects has completed the Chenhu Migratory Bird Observation Tower on Xianglushan, a natural rise within Wuhan’s Chenhu Wetland. Rising 19.8 meters (65 feet), the structure twists upward in two interlocking staircases to give visitors separate routes for ascending and descending while opening changing views across rivers and surrounding marshlands extending around them. The site already sits around 22 meters above sea level, so the climb begins among the trees before gradually lifting above the canopy and out toward the wetland horizon.
The observation tower draws that transition across the full ascent. Twenty-four staggered platforms interrupt the two spiraling routes, each one turning the body toward another portion of the landscape. A view that begins near leaves and branches, alongside the steel frame, gradually expands with height. Instead of saving the landscape for a single platform at the top, Xiang Architects extends the act of looking across the climb, with each turn changing what enters the frame.
The double helix also determines how the tower stands. Xiang Architects and structural designer AND Office developed an interlocking stair-support system that combines the stair flights with counter-rotating steel braces. Their opposing forces resist torsion without a conventional central core to leave a three-meter-wide opening running vertically through the structure. Seen from below, the void makes the overlapping stairs and braces legible as one continuous system.
The architects note that parametric modeling helped translate the geometry into 24 standardized modules that could be fabricated away from the wetland and assembled on site. The repetition gives a complex form a practical construction logic while reducing the amount of work taking place within the sensitive landscape. From inside, those repeated pieces create a dense field of diagonals that shifts with every step, sometimes framing the marsh beyond and sometimes pulling attention back toward the tower itself.
twin staircases twist in opposite directions around a three-meter open center
silver metal shifts with the wetland weather
A matte silver metal skin wraps the steel structure while keeping its edges open to air and views. Under gray skies, its surface takes on the pale tones of the wetland haze. Brighter conditions bring cooler reflections, while sunset draws warmer tones across the metal. Xiang Architects gives the tower a distinct presence on the hill, and the weather keeps changing how strongly its geometry reads against the landscape.
Chenhu Wetland becomes a winter habitat for more than 100,000 migratory birds each year between October and March. This gives the tower its wider purpose as an observation point. Its most engaging move happens before visitors reach the highest platform. By separating the two directions of travel and inserting viewing places throughout the climb, the architecture turns circulation itself into a way of scanning the wetland, one changing frame at a time.

twenty-four staggered platforms introduce changing views throughout the ascent
counter-rotating steel braces help the open structure resist torsion
parametric modeling rationalizes the complex geometry into 24 standardized modules

prefabricated components were assembled on site within the wetland landscape

Lionel Messi says he is retiring from the Argentina national soccer team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:46:26 UTC
00:46:26 KST

Lionel Messi says he is retiring from the Argentina national soccer team: "I leave with the peace of mind"
Soccer great Lionel Messi is hanging up his boots for the Argentina national team — ending nearly two decades representing the country.
Messi played in six World Cups and led Argentina to win the tournament in 2022 in Qatar. This summer, he and the Argentina squad made it to the final, losing to Spain.
"It was a decision that hurt — and still hurts deeply — but I understand that the time has come," Messi said in an Instagram post Monday. "I swear to you that I always gave it my all— not just in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too; I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football."
The announcement comes just weeks after his father, Jorge Messi, died on Aug. 8, at the age of 68.
In his post Monday, Messi explained that he wrote his retirement letter on June 21 — two days after losing the World Cup final at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
After his father's passing, Messi said he "didn't know how to keep going. All I ever did was play soccer and now I have serious doubts about whether I'll keep doing it for much longer."
On Monday he wrote, "Today, after everything with my dad, I am even more convinced than before."
The 39-year-old, who made his debut for Argentina's senior national team in 2006, thanked fans in his post on Monday.
"Thank you for all the love these past 20 years. I'm going to miss hearing you all from the inside so much. Now I'm going to be one of you, cheering and supporting you from the outside (through thick and thin, even more so)," Messi wrote.
"I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you — along with my teammates — moments we once only dreamed of. Experiencing this with you was incredible. I love you all," he added.
Messi played 207 games for Argentina and finishes as its all-time leading scorer with 125 goals — only long-time rival Cristiano Ronaldo has more goals, with 146, in men's internationals. Ronaldo has yet to announce his retirement from Portugal duty.
"Thank you for everything, Leo. Thank you for representing Argentina. Thank you for making us dream. Thank you for turning so many dreams into reality. The legend is yours, forever," the Argentine Football Association said in a statement.
Messi currently plays club soccer for Inter Miami after 17 seasons with Barcelona FC and a brief stint with Paris Saint-Germain. In his post, Messi did not say how long he will continue to play professional soccer.

Russia Has Quintupled Use of Jet-Powered Drones Against Ukraine, According to Yurii Ihnat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:44:34 UTC
00:44:34 KST

In July 2026, Russia increased its use of jet-powered UAVs against Ukraine fivefold compared with June.
On August 31, Yurii Ihnat, the Head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, stated this during a telethon, Interfax-Ukraine reports.
According to him, over the past four days, Ukrainian forces have recorded more than 1,500 drones, about 800 of which were jet-powered.
The overall effectiveness of Ukraine’s air defense was about 90%, but jet-powered UAVs were intercepted less frequently.
Ihnat noted that Russia began actively using jet-powered UAVs in July.
Over the course of a month, their number increased fivefold compared with June. Russian forces have also stepped up their use of Banderol-type UAVs, which combine the features of a drone and a missile.
According to the Air Force spokesperson, the new jet-powered UAVs are significantly harder to intercept due to their high speed.
Some of these vehicles can reach speeds of around 600 km/h, while Ukrainian interceptor drones currently reach approximately 300 km/h and physically cannot catch up with such targets.
Another challenge is the altitude at which jet-powered UAVs fly — around 5 km.
As a result, they operate beyond the effective engagement range of mobile fire teams and portable SAM systems.
Yurii Ihnat attributes the increased use of jet-powered UAVs to the high effectiveness of Ukrainian air defense against Shahed drones. According to him, Russia is attempting to shift to more complex and faster attack systems that require a wider range of interception capabilities.
This is also confirmed by the Russian military’s increased use of the S8000 Banderol cruise missile. Russia is currently producing the missile at a rate of approximately 80 units per month.
Experts classify the S8000 Bandrol as a small cruise missile or a jet-powered loitering munition that combines the features of a kamikaze drone and a missile. Its designers developed it with a focus on minimizing cost and simplifying production while retaining sufficient capabilities to strike targets at operational depth.
We also recommend reading this article on Militarnyi — “S8000 ‘Banderol’: A New Russian Missile for Strikes Against Ukraine.”
In appearance and aerodynamic configuration, the weapon resembles a miniature cruise missile, with a design that incorporates low-observability requirements. The fuselage is approximately 5 meters long, with a body diameter of around 30 centimeters. The missile features folding wings and stabilizers with a span of about 2.2 meters. This allows it to be transported in a folded configuration or mounted on the external pylons of aircraft carriers.
The small body diameter and use of composite materials reduce the target’s radar cross section. This makes it more difficult for radar stations to detect the missile, particularly when it flies at extremely low altitudes, where it can use the terrain for concealment.

Micronesian Islands Meet Against Backdrop of Great Power Competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:35:00 UTC
00:35:00 KST

From August 17 to 21, leaders and heads of delegation throughout the Micronesian subregion convened for the 28th Micronesian Islands Forum (MIF). Held in Pohnpei – one of four states of the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) and home to a population of roughly 26,000 people – delegates met to discuss ongoing regional issues and identified areas for strategic collaboration under the theme “Promote Healthy Communities, Open Doors to Learning.”
I attended the MIF as the head of Delegation and Special Representative for the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), a non-sovereign United States territory. As great powers pursue their foreign policy agendas, the event in Pohnpei revealed a continuing trend often overlooked in the Pacific: Micronesian governments are elevating unilateral hedging efforts in forums like the MIF, in pursuit of a unified risk-management strategy and regional identity.
This year, the MIF met weeks before the more prominent Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders Meeting, which is being held in the neighboring Micronesian country of Palau from August 30 to September 4. Seated in the front row of the forum’s audience were senior members of the diplomatic corps posted in the FSM, including ambassadors representing Australia, China, and Japan, and the United States’ newest Chargé d’Affaires to Palikir, who arrived in the country just a week before the MIF.
The venue itself was striking: the State of Pohnpei Administrative Building and Governor’s Office, built by Beijing in 2007 and renovated last year by the Chinese government and state-owned contractors. The Federated States of Micronesia have had formal diplomatic relations with Beijing since 1989, and is the only U.S. Freely Associated State – all of which are located in Micronesia – that maintains such a relationship.
China and the United States are not the only development partners competing in Pohnpei. Just two kilometers north of the Governor’s Office off the Dekehtik Causeway, Japan’s government is investing 4.6 billion yen ($30 million) in a project to expand the Pohnpei Port, the FSM’s primary maritime gateway. In the Pohnpeian outer island of Pingelap, Australia has financed a solar mini-grid and battery storage system for a geographically disconnected island community. These recent investments showcase the strategic importance of MIF member states to great powers and are not unique to FSM.
Similar practices can be found elsewhere across Micronesia. Foreign direct investment, infrastructure improvements, and diplomatic engagement have become increasingly visible in a region where small island economies are often balancing relationships with several development partners at once. For Micronesia, these relationships are not necessarily mutually exclusive. The same governments that have maintained a historically close partnership with the United States can pursue infrastructure and development partnerships with Japan, Australia, China, and others, depending on domestic needs and priorities.
The discussions held at the MIF centered around the outcomes of the forum’s several standing committees, including the approval of resolutions focused on U.S. deep sea mining efforts in Micronesia, the development of competitive commercial fisheries in Guam and the CNMI, and the financial stability of the forum itself. The latter action was arguably the most important to the MIF, functioning as a soft call to attending development partners and multilateral institutions for financial support. Member states underscored the need for sustainable funding to support a permanent secretariat, lifting the planning and implementation burden off of any future host government. The emphasis on establishing a more permanent institutional structure comes as Micronesian states continue to navigate their role within the broader Pacific regional infrastructure.
Five years ago, five Micronesian countries initiated the formal process to withdraw from the PIF after their supported candidate for the forum’s secretary-general position – a diplomat from the Marshall Islands – lost the body’s vote. The region instead decided to look inward, pursuing the strengthening of subregional collaboration. After reformation efforts in 2022 and 2023, those Micronesian nations rejoined the PIF, with the forum being held in the subregion for the first time since the 49th PIF in Nauru (now spelled Naoero) in 2018.
The history of that split remains relevant to the MIF today. The forum’s renewed focus on institutional sustainability is not only an administrative concern, but part of a broader effort to ensure that Micronesian governments have a regional mechanism through which they can coordinate their interests. Concurrently, the subregion’s reintegration into the PIF underscores that a robust MIF serves to complement, rather than contradict, expansive Pacific multilateralism.
This year’s PIF meeting further highlights the diplomatic complexity of Micronesia. Palau is hosting the meeting, with the Marshall Islands among the Micronesian states participating in the forum. Both countries maintain official diplomatic ties and a close relationship with Taiwan. Their participation comes as Micronesian governments continue to maintain contrasting relationships with the great powers active across the subregion, even as they pursue greater coordination on issues of common interest.
The timing of this year’s MIF, held two weeks before the PIF Leaders Meeting, provided an opportunity for Micronesian governments to coordinate ahead of the larger regional gathering. The standing committee outcomes raised in Pohnpei can be carried into discussions and actionable lines of effort in Palau. The proximity of the two meetings is particularly relevant this year, as the PIF returns to Micronesia.
For the MIF, member states must work diligently to make the regional forum in its 28th iteration more durable. The return of Micronesian states to the Pacific Islands Forum has restored their participation in the broader Pacific community, while the continued development of the Micronesian Islands Forum provides a concentrated platform for Micronesia’s concerns. How effectively the forum can maintain that balance will largely depend on whether its members and development partners can provide the resources required to sustain it.
The attention surrounding this year’s meetings suggests that the stakes are becoming higher. Micronesia is receiving more development assistance and greater strategic interest from external powers. As ministers, diplomats, and development partners switch gears from Pohnpei to Palau, and as U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau leads Washington’s delegation to the 55th PIF, one thing remains clear: all eyes are on Micronesia.
