India became ‘Vishwaguru’ through service, not pursuit of superpower status: RSS cheif Mohan Bhagwat in Toronto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:30:34 UTC
14:30:34 KST

India ‘vishwaguru’ through service, not pursuit of superpower status: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat in Toronto
Edited by: Ayush Pandey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 31, 2026, 12:22 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat in Toronto
RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat said India became a "Vishwaguru" (world teacher) through its selfless service to humanity rather than by becoming a "Mahashakti" (superpower), highlighting the country's civilisational tradition of friendship, refuge and respect for diversity.Addressing the "Hindu Vishwa Bandhu - Embrace the World in Friendship" gathering in Toronto, Bhagwat said India's global influence had historically come from sharing knowledge and extending help, rather than seeking territorial or political dominance."One may call Bharat a superpower, but it was not one. It served the world and by its own character, it became 'Vishwaguru', not Mahashakti," he said.
Bhagwat cited India's history of providing refuge to people fleeing persecution and conflict. Recalling the Second World War, he referred to the Maharaja of Jamnagar offering shelter and protection to Polish refugees until they could return safely."There are so many instances; it is still continuing," Bhagwat said.He also referred to India's evacuation efforts during conflicts in the Middle East, saying Indian military aircraft had rescued citizens of several countries alongside Indians."When, some years back in the Middle East war, people were trapped, the military planes of Bharat went there and rescued not only Bharatiya citizens; citizens of seven countries were rescued from there by Bharatiya," he said.
Bhagwat said India had historically provided peaceful refuge to Muslims, Christians, Jews and Parsis, arguing that those facing persecution could find asylum in the country."Anywhere in the world, if someone was persecuted, he got asylum in Bharat only," Bhagwat said.‘This is the tradition. This is the DNA of Bharat’The RSS chief contrasted India's civilisational outreach with imperial expansion, saying Indian travellers spread knowledge and values without conquering countries."Our ancestors travelled from Mexico to Siberia... They crossed the Himalayas on foot, went to Southeast Asia through small boats, but they conquered no country. They gave knowledge, astronomy, ayurveda, imparted civilisational values... Even today, when an ordinary Bharatiya goes to any country, the people there offer Namaskara," he added.He said helping people in distress was embedded in India's civilisational character and that the country had extended assistance even when help was not explicitly sought."This is the tradition. This is the DNA of Bharat," he said.Bhagwat also explained his understanding of the term Hindu, saying it should not be confined to a particular language, form of worship or lifestyle."When I say Hindu, the word Hindu cannot be defined by any specific language, through any specific worship, or through any living style," he said, adding that Hindus "respect all" and "accept all".He called for embracing diversity while recognising an underlying unity among humanity."We have to serve, accept, respect this diversity because it is an expression of unity. It beautifies it. It is the decoration. We celebrate it," he said.Bhagwat said India's ancient ethos viewed diversity as a natural feature of existence while considering unity to be the fundamental reality."There have been many castes, many creeds, many languages. Everything is many. Nothing""Nature, expression of reality, is diverse. Diversity is natural. Unity is the reality. You have to tackle with natural, keeping in mind reality. That is the ancient ethos of Bharat," he added.Invoking the philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, Bhagwat said an open-minded and knowledgeable person recognises the world as one family."Those who are open-minded and knowledgeable embrace the concept of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam--the belief that the entire earth is one family," he said.He said that despite differences in people's physical appearance, humanity was fundamentally united, making service to others a responsibility."Therefore, serving others is our duty. We have gained this wisdom, which brings us enduring happiness and satisfaction," Bhagwat said.
The address was delivered at the "Hindu Vishwa Bandhu - Embrace the World with Friendship" gathering, which brought together more than 2,000 members of Canada's Hindu community from all 10 provinces.The event was organised by CHORD, Canadian Hindus for Outreach, Relations and Dialogue, with support from more than 175 organisations. It focused on friendship, dialogue, belonging and shared responsibility, drawing on the Hindu civilisational ideal of "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam".

Google Maps Changes ‘Lake Ontario’ to ‘Lake America’ for U.S. Users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

U.S. users looking for Lake Ontario on Google Maps will now find “Lake America” in its place, after President Donald Trump’s executive order to rename the lake amid an escalating trade stoush.
Google announced Saturday that the lake, which borders the Canadian province of Ontario and the U.S. state of New York, will appear as “Lake America” in the U.S., “Lake Ontario” in Canada, and “Lake Ontario (Lake America)” for users in the rest of the world.
The company said it changed the maps following the formal renaming by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), and that the update is in line with its “long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”
The change has divided tech companies.
MapQuest, the first commercial web mapping service, said in a Thursday post, “We’re not changing the name of Lake Ontario. Name it whatever you want at your leisure.” The post included a link to a satirical tool allowing users to give the lake a name of their choosing and an image of a parody map labeling the body of water, “Lake Are We Doing This Again?”
As of Sunday, Apple had not changed the name on Apple Maps.
Lake Ontario/America
The change comes after Trump signed an executive order Thursday to officially rename the body of water—the latest salvo in an escalating trade war with Canada. After trade talks abruptly collapsed earlier this month, the U.S. and Canada announced tit-for-tat tariffs of up to 50% on some goods.
Canadian officials also called for Canadians to boycott U.S. travel and products, while Trump revived rhetoric of Canada being the “51st state” of the U.S., claiming that Canada wanted “the benefits of being a State, without being one.”
The name change has faced significant opposition from Democrats. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D, Mich.) announced plans to introduce the “Hands Off Our Great Lakes Act,” a bill that would reverse Trump’s order renaming the lake. Other Democratic lawmakers reportedly said they were preparing legislation to counter the name change.
Canadian officials also derided the name change. Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the renaming on Thursday, noting that Canadians will continue “calling it Lake Ontario—then, now and always.”
On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a newly erected 24-by-12-foot sign overlooking the lake in Winona, Ontario, that read “Lake Ontario Now and Always” in English and French.
Ford told ABC Sunday that the name change is “like something out of ‘Saturday Night Live.’”
“No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario. It’s just so disappointing,” he said.
Some Ontario government and business websites that use data from Google Maps showed “Lake America” after the change. A Google spokesperson told Axios that website developers embedding Google Maps can select a region to localize their maps.
“Following recent changes by Google, we’re actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario,” Stephen Crawford, Ontario’s minister of public and business service delivery and procurement, posted. “As Ontarians, we will always stand up for our province, our identity and the places that define it.”
Follows renaming Gulf of Mexico as the ‘Gulf of America’
Google made a similar change in February 2025 after Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” Google began displaying “Gulf of America” to Google Maps users in the U.S. after the name change was made in the U.S. federal geographic database.
Users in Mexico continued to see “Gulf of Mexico” and users elsewhere saw both names. Soon after, Apple Maps adopted the new name for U.S. users.
Mexico filed a lawsuit against Google in May 2025, arguing that the U.S. did not have the authority to rename the entire gulf, including waters under Mexican jurisdiction. The suit followed Google’s refusal to limit the “Gulf of America” label to the portion of the gulf under U.S. jurisdiction, as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum had requested. The lawsuit remains pending before the Superior Court of Justice of Mexico City.
Both Google and Apple also changed their U.S. map labels for North America’s highest peak from Denali to Mount McKinley last February. Trump had directed the name change in the same executive order, reversing a 2015 decision that had restored Denali, the mountain’s Alaska Native name, as its federal designation.
MapQuest retained the names of Denali and the Gulf of Mexico, and also offered users the option to rename the gulf as they pleased.

M+ Hong Kong Exhibition Traces Herzog & de Meuron's Design Process Across China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

An exhibition tracing the vision behind Herzog & de Meuron's ten selected projects in China will open on September 12, 2026, at the M+ Museum in Hong Kong. The exhibition marks the museum's fifth anniversary; since opening, M+ has built its collection around visual art, design and architecture, moving image, and Hong Kong visual culture from the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. The museum building, designed by Herzog & de Meuron between 2012 and 2021, is located in the city's West Kowloon Cultural District (WestK), a cultural hub spanning forty hectares alongside Victoria Harbour. "Herzog & de Meuron: In Focus" is curated by Ikko Yokoyama and Iris Ng and reviews projects dating from 2002 to 2021, including Tai Kwun in Hong Kong (2006–2018) and the National Stadium in Beijing (2002–2008).
The exhibition marks the second phase of Herzog & de Meuron's donation to the M+ Collections, building on the first contribution of a section model of the Beijing National Stadium (2002–2008), known as the 'Bird's Nest', in 2023. On this occasion, the office provided the museum with more than 200 process materials, including models, prototypes, sketches, and archival items. "Herzog & de Meuron: In Focus" shows the material behind ten built and unbuilt projects from the early 2000s, marking the firm's sustained participation in China's growth and urban transformation through landmark cultural and civic projects including museums, academic institutions, sports stadiums and city master plans.
The objects and replicas are displayed in wooden vitrines developed for the firm's open storage of archival holdings in Basel, Switzerland, in a design inspired by the firm's Kabinett. Kabinett is a foundation established in 2015 by Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron as a permanent repository of architectural thinking and knowledge for research and exchange. The process and archival materials provided by the architects are intended to give the public an overview of each building's response to site, materials, and cultural context. The exhibition brings together models, drawings, material samples and prototypes donated to the M+ Collection to "offer a closer look into the perspectives that shape the firm's architectural imagination."
 Focusing on ten pivotal projects in China, this exhibition traces both the evolving creative vision that defines Herzog & de Meuron's practice and the wider transformation of China's urban landscape. The open-storage display, inspired by the Kabinett, repositions the gallery as a space for discovery and dialogue. By showcasing the models, materials, methods, and research of these important architectural projects, we invite visitors to explore the experimentation and decision-making behind each work, from early ideas to built form. ― Ikko Yokoyama, Senior Curator, Head of Design and Architecture at M+
The exhibition will be on view from September 12, 2026, to January 2027 at the M+ Focus Gallery. The museum will also organize an architecture tour throughout the exhibition period for visitors to discover the museum's distinctive architectural features and design highlights. Also in China, Shanghai's Power Station of Art (PSA) will host the country's first exhibition dedicated to the work of Brazilian architect Lina Bo Bardi, designed by OPEN Architecture in a 2,300 m² space of the PSA contemporary art museum in Huangpu. In Australia, OPEN Architecture also joined OMA/AMO in designing one of the opening exhibitions of Powerhouse Parramatta, the first state cultural organization located in Western Sydney. On a larger scale, the 9th edition of the Oslo Architecture Triennale will take place from September 17 to October 1, bringing together more than 30 international architecture projects around the question "What if Nature Comes First?"

Taiwan military says China amphibious assault capacity still limited
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:01:06 UTC
14:01:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Beijing still lacks sufficient amphibious landing capabilities, the Ministry of National Defense said in its 2026 report on Chinese military power released on Monday.
The ministry said that amphibious operations are among the most complex military tasks for the PLA, Liberty Times reported. They require simultaneous multi-point landings, air and sea superiority, and sustained troop and logistics support, the ministry said.
Though current PLA capabilities remain insufficient, amphibious forces continue to train alongside naval and airborne units, the ministry warned. It said that the PLA is also incorporating civilian roll-on/roll-off ferries, cargo ships, and semi-submersible vessels into joint landing exercises with amphibious and army aviation forces, per Liberty Times.
China continues to develop new bridge-type amphibious landing craft and amphibious ships to bolster landing and logistics capabilities, the ministry said.
In terms of gray zone activities, Chinese military aircraft and drones continuously fly across the Taiwan Strait median line and into Taiwan’s air defense identification zone, the ministry said, according to Liberty Times. Meanwhile, Chinese naval vessels sail near Taiwan to conduct joint combat readiness patrols, it said.
The ministry pointed out that China uses military exercises to intimidate Taiwan.
Through its cyber warfare forces, China integrates resources and continues to invest in technology and personnel to strengthen capabilities for cyberattacks and malware deployment, the ministry said, per Liberty Times. China regards cyberspace as a key domain of modern warfare, adopting a model of peacetime infiltration and wartime disruption, it said.
The ministry added that the PLA integrates firepower resources across branches to establish a joint strike system. Depending on mission requirements, it has targets set on key military facilities and critical infrastructure in Taiwan.
China focuses on saturation and surprise attacks to disrupt Taiwan's command and communications, air defense, and logistics.

Chiu echoed Ko’s demand for Hsu to address the issue, saying that speaking through spokespersons does not adequately convey her sincerity, per UDN. He said the TPP is under immense pressure from its supporters over the situation.
Huang noted that while he has not heard from Cheng or other high-ranking KMT officials, Hsinchu County Magistrate Yang Wen-ke (楊文科) has conveyed his concerns about the development, per NOWNews. He stressed that trust built up through years of cooperation could be destroyed by one wrong move.
Huang also said some KMT lawmakers had phoned him to express support for Chiu. He urged TPP supporters to limit their response to the controversy to Hsinchu County and not affect other areas where KMT officials have kept their promises to the TPP.
Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) urged the two parties to continue cooperating, stressing that the coalition will hold in Taichung, per Liberty Times. Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) urged the parties to continue negotiations to maximize opportunities for cooperation.
The KMT reportedly conducted an internal survey of the Zhubei mayoral race, showing Wu leading Chiu by double digits, per UP Media. However, a TPP internal survey conducted in early August showed Chiu had cut the gap to within the margin of error.
A KMT insider suggested that, since the party has already put forward a mayoral candidate, Chiu would need to compete with Wu in polling to secure the opposition ticket. A local KMT campaign source suggested that limited movement in Chiu’s polling numbers, along with the importance of Zhubei, led the KMT to put forward its own candidate, per UDN.
Soochow University Assistant Professor Chang Yuan-hsiang (張元祥) suggested that the breakdown in cooperation highlighted the two parties’ inability to work together outside official frameworks, per SETN. He argued that if neither party is willing to compromise, the trust built up between the two parties could be damaged.

Rocky planets may have formed just 100 million years after the Big Bang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Rocky planets may have formed just 100 million years after the Big Bang
The ingredients for rocky, potentially habitable planets may have appeared just 100 million years after the Big Bang, billions of years earlier than scientists once expected.
- Date:
- August 31, 2026
- Source:
- University of Portsmouth
- Summary:
- Rocky planets may have been able to start forming just 100 million years after the Big Bang, thanks to enormous early supernovae that scattered planet-building elements across space. Simulations found enough solid material and water around a young star to suggest that Earth-like worlds could have appeared far earlier than previously believed.
- Share:
The ingredients needed to build rocky planets may have appeared as early as 100 million years after the Big Bang, according to new research from the University of Portsmouth. That would place the beginnings of planet formation remarkably close to the dawn of the Universe, even before the first galaxies had fully emerged.
Scientists have long thought that planets took much longer to become possible, with significant planet formation beginning several billion years into cosmic history. The new findings suggest that the necessary conditions may have developed far sooner.
The First Stars Seeded Space With Planet Ingredients
Some of the earliest stars were extremely massive and ended their lives in violent explosions. These stellar blasts spread large quantities of elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron into the surrounding gas.
Known as 'Pop III supernovae', these explosions acted as the Universe's first major sources of the heavier elements required to make planets and, eventually, life.
Dr. Daniel Whalen, from the University of Portsmouth's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation, said: "Our new paper, in which my PhD student Chris Jessop ran the first part of the simulation chain, shows that the precursors of terrestrial planets can form around low-mass, long-lived stars in the debris of the first cosmic explosions 100 million years after the Big Bang.
"To put this into perspective, the Universe is about 13.8 billion years old, so this is remarkably early in cosmic history."
Powerful Supernovae Could Create Planet-Forming Disks
One especially energetic kind of Pop III supernova, called a pair-instability supernova, can eject more than 100 times the Sun's mass in heavy elements during a single explosion.
That material can dramatically increase the abundance of heavy elements in nearby clouds of gas. As gravity pulls those enriched clouds together, they can form rotating disks around young stars, similar to the disk of material that eventually produced our own Solar System.
Dr. Whalen added: "In our computer simulations of the early Universe, we found one such disc around a young star about 70 percent as massive as the Sun. Within that disc, enough solid material accumulated to create several Earth-masses' worth of planetary building blocks at roughly the same distance from the star as Earth is from the Sun.
Water Was Already Present
The simulations revealed another striking feature: the disk contained a substantial supply of water.
"Most surprisingly, the disc also contained substantial amounts of water, only a few times less than what was available when our own Solar System formed. This means that any planets forming there could potentially have received water in a similar way to Earth, which is thought to have gained much of its water from material left over during the planet-building process.
"Our findings suggest that the conditions for planet formation may have existed much earlier than previously thought. If that's the case, it raises an intriguing question: could potentially habitable worlds have appeared far earlier in the Universe's history as well?"
The findings suggest that rocky planets, and possibly worlds with some of the ingredients associated with habitability, may have become possible much earlier in cosmic history than scientists previously expected.
The paper is published in The Astrophysical Letters Journal.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Portsmouth. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Eduard I. Vorobyov, Daniel J. Whalen, Muhammad A. Latif, Alexander Skliarevskii, Christopher Jessop, Ryoki Matsukoba, Takashi Hosokawa, Devesh Nandal. Planet Formation at Cosmic Dawn: Planetesimals in H2O-rich Disks around Low-mass Stars. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2026; 1007 (2): L51 DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/ae907c

Chinese sci-fi, digital cultural IPs shine at Worldcon in California
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:49:57 CST
13:49:57 KST

A visitor views exhibits during the 84th World Science Fiction Convention (Worldcon) at the Anaheim Convention Center in Orange County, California, the United States, on Aug. 29, 2026. Chinese science fiction and digital cultural intellectual properties (IPs) and products from Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, have drawn wide attention at the ongoing 84th Worldcon in Southern California.(Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua)
LOS ANGELES, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese science fiction and digital cultural intellectual properties (IPs) and products from Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, have drawn wide attention at the ongoing 84th World Science Fiction Convention (Worldcon) in Southern California.
This year's convention, running from Aug. 27 to 31 at the Anaheim Convention Center in Orange County, Southern California, brings together thousands of fans, authors, artists, actors, scientists, and lovers of science fiction and fantasy from around the globe.
A lineup of sci-fi and digital cultural IPs and products from Chengdu is on show at the convention, including KORMO, the mascot of the 2023 Worldcon, Walulu, All Wishes Came True!, Doctor Who merchandise, and PANDA HOMELAND Heaney.
Robert J. Sawyer, a renowned Canadian science fiction writer and Hugo and Nebula Awards winner, depicted the sci-fi and digital cultural IPs from Chengdu as "highlights" of Chinese innovation at the convention.
Having visited China seven times, Sawyer told Xinhua that he has witnessed the rapid growth of China's sci-fi community.
"It's fantastic to see this becoming so popular ... to see young people reading about science, technology, computers, artificial intelligence, exploring the solar system, going beyond the solar system," Sawyer told Xinhua.
On the innovation and writing styles of Chinese science fiction writers, Sawyer said that they are writing exciting scientific breakthroughs in the way Western science fiction writers used to, but with all the technology and science available today, including computing, quantum physics, space travel and biotechnology.
He also highlighted the diversity of China's sci-fi culture, including Chinese artwork, graphic novels, computer-animated videos, films and television productions.
Considering international exchanges important to the development of science fiction, he said that writers and editors from China, Canada, Europe and the United States have been working together on projects that bring different perspectives on the future.
Carolina Gomez Lagerlof, chair of the European Science Fiction Society, told Xinhua that interest in Chinese science fiction has grown considerably in Western Europe in recent years and that an increasing number of Chinese science fiction works are now available in translation.
She said she was also surprised by the scale of interest in science fiction in China after visiting the country and meeting Chinese fans.
Chen Shi, secretary-general of Chengdu Science Fiction Society, said the sci-fi community in Chengdu hopes to showcase the appeal of Chinese sci-fi at the convention, learn from Hollywood's experience in innovation and development in the sci-fi sector, and further strengthen exchanges and cooperation with the international sci-fi community.
Since its founding in 1939, Worldcon has become the annual gathering of the World Science Fiction Society and one of science fiction's most important cultural events. Its Hugo Award rank among the field's most coveted prizes for science fiction and fantasy. ■

China's manufacturing PMI at 49.8 in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:49:44 CST
13:49:44 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The purchasing managers' index (PMI) for China's manufacturing sector stood at 49.8 in August, up 0.6 percentage points from July, official data showed Monday.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 indicates contraction.
In August, the manufacturing sector's overall business climate saw notable improvement, said Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the National Bureau of Statistics, citing that among the 21 industries surveyed, 16 reported a higher PMI compared with the previous month.
This sector saw expansion in both manufacturing output and market demand in August. The production sub-index and new orders index climbed to 50.4 and 50.6, up 0.5 percentage points and 2.1 percentage points from July.
Driven by the pick-up in both production and orders, enterprises' willingness to purchase strengthened, with the procurement volume index reaching 50.5, up 1.1 percentage points from the previous month, said Huo.
The development momentum of new growth drivers continued to improve in August, she said.
The PMI for the equipment manufacturing industry and the high-tech manufacturing industry stood at 51.4 and 52.9, respectively, both remaining in the expansion zone.
Affected by recent upward movements in crude oil and non-ferrous metal prices, the purchasing price index for major raw materials and the ex-factory price index for manufacturing stood at 56.6 and 50.4, respectively, up 3.4 percentage points and 2.6 percentage points from the previous month.
The PMI for large manufacturing enterprises came in at 50.6, up 1.1 percentage points from the previous month and returning to the expansion zone. ■

The baby whom Razia Noreen saved was the sole survivor of a fire that killed 14 other infants at a major government hospital in Islamabad
Fire engulfed Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, a major government hospital in Islamabad, on Wednesday. A 51-second segment of CCTV footage, widely circulated online, captures Razia Noreen running into the burning nursery and emerging seconds later with the newborn in her arms. She tries to go back in, but cannot because of the flames and thick smoke.

The City of Copenhagen is ready to send more displaced Ukrainians to Jutland after five Jutland mayors opposed the government’s bill to halt immigration from 14 Ukrainian regions in Jyllands-Posten.
Andreas Keil, Social Democrats, Mayor of Employment, Integration, and Business, wrote this in a letter to the mayors.
“If you have the opportunity to receive a number of displaced Ukrainians, it will be a great help to Copenhagen,” he wrote in the letter.
He further writes that it will simultaneously be a concrete contribution to the redistribution among municipalities that Minister for Immigration and Integration Morten Bødskov (Social Democrats as well) has previously requested.
“I understand it to mean that the five Jutland municipalities would like more settlement, labor, and have more opportunities to accommodate the newcomers, while we, conversely, in Copenhagen are challenged to find accommodation for more than the 3,800 Ukrainians we already accommodate now,” he stated.
The letter has been sent to the mayors of Hjørring, Lemvig, Vesthimmerland, Skive, and Brønderslev Municipality, respectively.

Coral bleaching occurring too frequently for reefs to recover, scientists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:30:00 UTC
13:30:00 KST

Coral bleaching occurring too frequently for reefs to recover, scientists say
- Coral reefs are bleaching more often, now every five to six years, leaving no time for recovery and causing a sharp decline in global coral cover.
- The 2023 bleaching event was the largest recorded, affecting 77 per cent of reefs, with rising ocean temperatures and El Nino increasing future risks.
- Immediate action is needed to reduce emissions and manage local threats to prevent irreversible coral loss and protect marine ecosystems and livelihoods.
AI generated
SYDNEY/SINGAPORE – Coral reefs are experiencing bleaching events so frequently that they no longer have time to recover before the next one strikes, with global coral cover now well below normal levels and at risk of irreversible decline, scientists said on Aug 31.
The world’s coral reefs sustain a quarter of all marine life, make coastlines more resilient and provide food and livelihoods for millions of people, but their survival has been threatened by pollution and increasingly frequent mass bleaching caused by soaring ocean heat.
The gap between bleaching events once stretched for decades, but now averages just five or six years, a group of scientists known as the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network said in a report based on more than 40 years of data from nearly 37,000 reef sites in 120 countries and territories.
“If we give them enough time, they have the capacity to recover,” lead author Manuel Gonzalez Rivero said. “But we haven’t seen that amount of time being allowed. In fact, the frequency of those bleaching events has pretty much doubled.”
Bleaching occurs when corals expel the colourful algae living in their tissues. Without the algae delivering nutrients to the corals, they become pale and vulnerable to starvation and disease. While a bleached coral is not dead, ocean temperatures need to cool off if it is to have any hope of recovery.
The report’s release comes as Pacific leaders gather in Palau on Aug 31 for the annual Pacific Islands Forum. The leaders are expected to coordinate climate priorities before the COP31 climate conference later in 2026.
Its findings provide further evidence of the impact that climate change is having on fragile coral reef ecosystems, with hard coral cover shrinking 9.5 per cent below the historical average over 2020 to 2024.
“We had 40 years of coral cover around the world that had remained relatively unchanged until 2010,” Gonzalez Rivero said.
“Since 2010, there has been a very steep change.”
‘Staircase of decline’
Scientists recorded the world’s first mass bleaching event in 1998, and three more have occurred since 2010.
When temperatures fall, reefs can recover relatively quickly. From 2017 to 2019, reefs gained 6 per cent coral cover, nearly offsetting the 6.6 per cent loss from the 2016 bleaching event.
The latest bleaching in 2023 was the most extensive on record, impacting 77 per cent of the world’s coral reef areas, part of what Gonzalez Rivero described as a “staircase of decline”.
With El Nino weather patterns intensifying and the daily global average sea-surface temperature reaching a record high of 21.1 deg C on Aug 22, another bleaching event could strike the world’s reefs in 2026, he said. “It is very likely, given the temperatures.”
Rapid cuts in emissions and the management of local threats – including unsustainable fishing and excessive coastal development – could limit further losses, the report said.
“We must act now to halt this decline and invest in solutions that reduce pressures and build resilience,” said David Obura, chairman of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services.
“Delayed action risks locking in irreversible losses.” REUTERS

Philippine Peso Slumps to Record Low Amid Rising Energy Prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:27:00 UTC
13:27:00 KST

The Philippine peso fell to a record low on Friday due to rising oil prices and a strengthening U.S. dollar, despite attempts by the country’s central bank to offer relief.
According to a report by Inquirer.net, which cited data from Bankers Association of the Philippines, the currency weakened 37.7 centavos to close at 62.265 per U.S. dollar, surpassing the previous record-low close of 61.888 set the day prior.
The new record capped off three straight weeks of losses for the peso, which has been among the Asian currencies most vulnerable to the spike in energy prices brought about by the war in the Middle East. The peso has lost nearly 8 percent since the Iran war began on February 28, due in large part to the Philippines’ heavy reliance on oil imports, which has contributed to rising inflation.
This came despite a decision by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas to raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points point to 5 percent. Central bank Governor Eli Remolona Jr. described the increase, which brought the total increase in the current anti-inflation campaign to 75 basis points, as a “preemptive” move against emerging inflation risks. Philippine policymakers now expect inflation to average 6.1 percent this year, and 5.4 percent in 2027, up from a decade-long low of 1.7 percent in 2025 and 3.2 percent in 2024.
Citi analysts told Reuters that the outlook for the currency remained negative, “due to significant external pressures.”
“The current-account deficit is widening, driven by elevated energy prices and a weaker services balance in the recent quarter,” the analysts stated. “This pressure could persist, as future government infrastructure spending would keep the import bill elevated.”
Among Asian currencies, the other major casualty of the Iran war has been the Indonesian rupiah, which fell by around 8 percent in the first six months of 2026, and in early June sunk to a record low of 18,190 against the dollar – lower than even during the depths of the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998.
The currency has been under pressure since President Prabowo Subianto came to office in October 2024, promising high-spending social programs that sent a tremor of concern through the markets. However, these concerns have only bene compounded by the economic reverberations of the Iran war.
The Thai baht has also weakened, falling to 32.96 to the U.S. dollar at the close of its last session, down 4.6 percent since the start of 2026.
The immediate impacts of the weak peso are likely to be mixed. As Inquirer.net reported, millions of families will benefit from the fact that remittances from relatives abroad will be worth more locally, potentially giving households greater spending power. Exporters may also benefit as a weaker currency makes Philippine goods more competitive overseas.
However, it noted that a weaker peso “also raises the cost of imported goods, while companies and the government face higher peso costs when repaying foreign-currency debt.”

Scientists discover diamonds can generate electricity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:13:53 UTC
13:13:53 KST

Scientists discover diamonds can generate electricity
- Date:
- August 31, 2026
- Source:
- The University of Hong Kong
- Summary:
- Diamond was thought to be incapable of producing electricity through mechanical deformation, but ultrathin flexible diamond membranes have now shown a strong and repeatable piezoelectric effect. The unexpected discovery could open the door to diamond-powered sensors, tiny energy systems, and self-powered medical implants.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have discovered that ultrathin, highly flexible diamond membranes can produce a measurable piezoelectric response, challenging a scientific assumption that has stood for more than a century.
The work was led by Professor Zhiqin Chu, Associate Professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, and Professor Yuan Lin, Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering at the University of Hong Kong (HKU).
Diamond Breaks a Century-Old Rule
Since the early 1900s, diamond has generally been classified as a non-piezoelectric material, meaning it was not expected to generate an electrical voltage when mechanically deformed.
That limitation has shaped how diamond has been used in engineering. Despite its exceptional hardness, strength, chemical stability, high acoustic velocity, thermal conductivity, dielectric breakdown strength and ultrawide bandgap, diamond has typically served only as a structural support for other piezoelectric materials in microelectromechanical systems (MEMS).
For that reason, the idea of "generating electricity from diamonds" was long considered impractical.
Making Diamond Thin Enough To Bend
To test whether diamond could behave differently under extreme mechanical conditions, the HKU team used a recently developed edge exfoliation method to produce an ultrathin, flexible polycrystalline diamond membrane.
Reducing the material to such a thin form allowed the normally rigid diamond to bend much more than bulk diamond can. When the researchers deliberately flexed the membrane, they observed stable voltage signals.
The team then carried out extensive mechanical cycling experiments under carefully controlled conditions to make sure the electrical output was genuine. These tests were designed to rule out environmental interference and triboelectric effects, which can generate electrical signals when surfaces contact or rub against one another.
The voltage appeared consistently and repeatedly, providing strong evidence that the diamond membrane itself was producing a piezoelectric response.
Grain Boundaries Create the Electrical Effect
To understand why the effect occurs, the researchers performed detailed first-principles calculations.
Their analysis points to asymmetry at the grain boundaries inside the polycrystalline diamond membrane. These boundaries separate the many tiny diamond crystals that make up the material.
As the membrane bends more strongly, electrical charge polarization builds up around those grain boundaries. This creates a difference in electrical potential between the upper and lower surfaces of the membrane, producing the observed voltage.
Potential for Medical Devices and Tiny Power Systems
The discovery could open new possibilities for diamond in areas where durability and safety are especially important.
Diamond is highly biocompatible, chemically stable, and non-toxic, making it attractive for both medical and energy-related technologies. In the future, piezoelectric diamond membranes could potentially be used in implantable medical devices as self-generating power sources or as sensors that detect bending and deformation.
More broadly, the findings introduce a new way to give diamond active electrical functionality rather than using it only as a passive structural material.
The work could also support the development of next-generation high-reliability micro energy systems and self-powered sensing technologies.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The University of Hong Kong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jixiang Jing, Bicong Wang, Yumeng Luo, Yicheng Wang, Zhongqiang Wang, Yiyao Liu, Dong-Keun Ki, Xinghua Shi, Qi Wang, Kwai Hei Li, Yuan Lin, Zhiqin Chu. Uncovering piezoelectric effect in polycrystalline diamond membranes. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (12) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aea8318

Taiwan’s Topco Scientific and Scivax team up on optical components

Unknown Publisher

04:07:20 UTC
13:07:20 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Topco Scientific Co. said Monday it is partnering with Japanese nanoimprint lithography specialist Scivax to mass produce optical components used in co-packaged optics (CPO).
Topco CEO Chen Te-yi (陳德義) said traditional copper interconnects face increasing bandwidth and power-consumption challenges as AI and HPC workloads generate more data, per UDN. He said CPO can address those constraints by shortening electrical transmission distances while improving bandwidth density and energy efficiency.
The companies plan to showcase their technologies at SEMICON Taiwan on Sept. 4. Scivax’s technology can replicate complex optical surfaces onto wafers and is designed for microlens arrays and waveguides.
The collaboration also incorporates optical materials from Japan’s Shin-Etsu Chemical Co., which are used in Scivax’s microlens arrays, UDN reported. The materials offer heat resistance and high optical-signal coupling efficiency, while testing has shown the lenses can withstand thermal stress.
Scivax operates two wafer foundry facilities in Toyama, Japan, and the company says they have a combined monthly capacity of up to 8,000 8-inch wafers, per Next Apple. Its substrate-free microlens arrays can be made less than 60 micrometers thick, supporting small optical designs and reducing optical crosstalk.

Taiwan military aligns more closely with US combat practices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:07:18 UTC
13:07:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US is increasingly influencing Taiwan’s combat tactics and equipment, according to a Business Insider report.
Chieh Chung (揭仲), a senior analyst at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, told Business Insider that Taiwan is following more US recommendations on training, target identification and strikes, and special forces operations.
"This makes it necessary for the US side to observe live exercises to assess the effectiveness and shortcomings of its recommendations and of bilateral military exchanges, providing a basis for subsequent adjustments and revisions," Chieh said.
This year’s Han Kuang exercises introduced the “backbrief” for the first time, per Business Insider. It is a US military practice in which junior commanders relay their understanding of a mission and its orders to their superiors.
Taiwan is now adopting it as part of efforts to train and authorize lower-level commanders to make their own decisions if communication with superiors is lost.
Lin Ping-yu (林秉宥), New Taipei City councilor and former Taiwanese special forces paratrooper, said, "This highlights an area where Taiwan's military culture urgently needs to evolve," according to Business Insider.
"The traditional mindset of 'mission accomplished at all costs' is ill-suited to modern battlefields," he added.
When asked about US military presence during the Han Kuang exercise, a US State Department spokesperson told Business Insider that the US remains committed to its “one China” policy and to maintaining peace in the Taiwan Strait.
The spokesperson did not confirm if there are military personnel on the ground. However, they said the US helps provide Taiwan with the necessary arms and related support to defend itself.
Some of those weapons were featured during the Han Kuang exercise, including Patriot missiles, M1A2 Abrams tanks, F-16Vs, and High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems, according to Business Insider. Taiwanese troops were also seen launching Anduril’s Altius 600M loitering munitions during drills.
Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey said in June that he hopes to expand manufacturing in Taiwan.
Earlier this month, Taiwan Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said that Taiwan-US military cooperation “is far closer than you might imagine,” per a Wall Street Journal report. “The public sees only the arms sales, but in fact, it’s multifaceted and involves so much more,” he said.
“Through military exchanges, we have been learning so much practical combat experience from the US,” Koo said. However, the defense minister stressed that Taiwan’s plan for a potential cross-strait conflict does not rely on US military intervention, WSJ reported.

Water Resources Agency criticized for failure to update Taiwan river management plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:07:16 UTC
13:07:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Water Resources Agency rejected Sunday the National Audit Office’s criticism of its failure to update river management plans, stressing that its management rate for rivers under its jurisdiction has reached 91.25%.
The National Audit Office noted in its report that, of the 183 rivers and tributaries under central government jurisdiction, 50% have not had their management plans updated in 10 years, with major flooding occurring in 11 of them, per UDN. The office suggested that without updating management plans, as required by existing regulations, the government cannot effectively evaluate whether flood mitigation capacity and standards are correct.
The office pointed out that Mataian Creek, which saw a catastrophic barrier lake overflow last year, last had its management plan updated in 2013. It called on the agency to update the plan so necessary flood mitigation projects and adjustments can be made.
KMT Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) noted that Taiwan has seen an increase in the frequency and intensity of heavy rainfall, per UDN. She called for a comprehensive review of Taiwan’s flood mitigation measures and the cost-effectiveness of related investments in southern Taiwan.
Central Weather Administration official Lo Tzu-ting (羅資婷) told The Reporter that a review of daily precipitation data between 1960 and 2023 revealed that the frequency of heavy rainfall events increased between the first and second 30-year periods, with Kaohsiung seeing a more significant increase than Taipei. Administration official Chen Meng-shih (陳孟詩) pointed to climate change and rising temperatures, adding that Taiwan has seen a greater increase in precipitation intensity than the global average.
The Water Resources Agency rejected the assessment, noting that its river management rate and drainage regulation rate had reached 91.25% and 79.7%, respectively, per NOWNews. It argued that analyzing whether flood mitigation standards fit the needs on the ground, changes to river courses, and other factors are more important than simply updating river management plans.
The agency noted that flooding incidents over the past three years have mostly resulted from existing drainage infrastructure being unable to cope with intense rainfall. It added that flooding caused by rivers or drainage system overflows has not increased significantly.
The agency stressed that if significant changes in river systems are identified after flooding, such as the Mataian Creek barrier lake overflow, it will review its plans, per KNews. The agency said recent intense precipitation in southern Taiwan has exceeded the design capacity of the drainage systems, necessitating investments to lessen the impacts of future flooding incidents.

US aerospace society recognizes Taiwan-Japan CubeSat for imaging capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:06:43 UTC
13:06:43 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The CubeSat “OnglaiSat” won the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA) Small Satellite Mission of the Year award during the Small Satellite Conference held in the US last week.
The satellite is a collaboration between the Taiwan Space Agency (TASA), the University of Tokyo’s ISSL aerospace laboratory, Japanese satellite company ArkEdge Space, and Space BD, a Japanese space business and services firm, CNA reported. TASA developed the Korsch optical payload, while the University of Tokyo developed the 6U CubeSat platform.
A CubeSat is a type of cost-effective nanosatellite used for missions, such as scientific research and testing new technologies, according to NASA. They can also be used in constellations or swarms for advanced missions.
Measuring 6U (30 × 20 × 10 cm), the OnglaiSat was recognized by AIAA for successfully validating high-end optical and imaging control technologies on such a small platform. The achievement marks a new milestone in the commercialization of global microsatellite constellations and high-frequency, high-resolution Earth observation, per CNA. It is also the first time a space mission developed by Japanese and Taiwanese teams has received this honor.
The satellite was launched into low Earth orbit from the International Space Station in December 2024. It successfully captured images in early 2025 and completed more than 100 imaging missions within about two months of initial operations, according to CNA.
TASA said that the satellite integrates a high-precision attitude determination and control system with an advanced optical remote sensing payload to take images with a ground resolution of 2.44 meters. Using time-delay integration imaging technology, it achieved a signal-to-noise ratio above 100.
Its achievement demonstrates the potential of small, low-cost satellites to perform high-resolution optical Earth observation missions, TASA added.

====================================================================================================

Column: SCO at 25: a model for new type of int'l relations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:57:09 CST
12:57:09 KST

by Al Mamun Harun Ur Rashid
As the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) enters its 25th year, the international system stands at an important historical crossroads, marked by escalating geopolitical tensions and zero-sum thinking. While Western countries erect exclusive blocs to deter the Global South and preserve their superpower dominance, China actively advances the SCO, not a military alliance, but a platform of partnership and mutual cooperation to build a community with a shared future for humanity.
Established in Shanghai on June 15, 2001, by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, the SCO evolved from the Shanghai Five mechanism. India and Pakistan joined in 2017, Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024, bringing its full membership to 10 countries.
What began as a Central Asian security mechanism now spans Eurasia, covering security, trade, transport, energy, agriculture, science, education, health and culture. It is neither a military alliance nor an economic bloc, but a platform for cooperation among states with mutually diverse interests and foreign policies.
This expansion reflects the magnetic appeal of the "Shanghai Spirit," which rejects exclusive alliances to practice "harmony without uniformity." It provides an institutional space where diverse nations cooperate on an equal footing while fully preserving their strategic autonomy and distinctive development paths.
The China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has also become an important element of economic discussions within the organization. Several SCO members have supported efforts to connect BRI projects with other regional economic initiatives, including the Eurasian Economic Union. It is estimated that the combined economic aggregate of the SCO member states stands at close to 30 trillion U.S. dollars.
Countries across Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East have increasingly called for greater representation in global decision-making, particularly in institutions whose structures were established under different geopolitical and economic conditions.
At the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization Plus" Meeting on Sept. 1, 2025, Chinese President Xi Jinping emphasized taking actions to uphold international fairness and justice, urging member states to oppose hegemonism and power politics. This stance reinforces the SCO's role as a pillar of global governance reform.
Beyond security, the SCO is developing financial cooperation, including greater use of national currencies and financing mechanisms. The New Development Bank, though a BRICS institution rather than an SCO body, reflects the expanding Global South development finance architecture, with 42.9 billion U.S. dollars approved for 139 projects by the end of 2025.
The SCO's expanding network of partner countries also gives non-members channels for engagement on trade, transport, energy, tourism, education and other issues.
For regional countries such as Bangladesh, the SCO's significance can therefore be viewed through the prism of connectivity and economic development.
Bangladesh does not need to choose between competing geopolitical camps to engage with emerging Eurasian institutions. Its interests could include greater access to Central Asian markets, transport connectivity, energy cooperation, food security, digital development and wider South-South economic links.
The 25-year journey of the SCO proves to the world that a more representative and balanced international order is entirely achievable.
The SCO has already demonstrated that countries with respective interests can maintain a common institutional framework. Its next challenge is to translate that political durability into more measurable gains in trade, connectivity, development, security and people-to-people cooperation.
Editor's note: Al Mamun Harun Ur Rashid is a diplomatic correspondent at The New Nation, a leading English-language mainstream newspaper in Bangladesh. He covers Bangladesh's foreign policy, diplomacy, regional affairs and international relations, with a particular focus on China, the broader Asia-Pacific region and the Global South.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

SEOUL, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's national tax revenue grew in July on the back of surging stock trades and inflows of value-added tax (VAT), the finance ministry said Monday.
The tax revenue totaled 51 trillion won (37.1 billion U.S. dollars) in July, up 8.4 trillion won compared to the same month of last year, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy.
The VAT inflows jumped 3.2 trillion won in the cited month, driven by a growth in final VAT filings for the first half of 2026 and robust import expansion.
The country's imports surged 26.5 percent from a year earlier to 68.57 billion dollars in July.
Revenue from the securities transaction tax added 1.1 trillion won, while the special tax for rural development, levied on stock transactions, mounted 2 trillion won last month.
The expansion was backed by a spike in trading volumes of listed stocks, which skyrocketed 232.4 percent over the year to 2,087.2 trillion won in June.
The collection of income tax climbed 1.8 trillion won in July from a year earlier, supported by higher payroll payouts alongside a recovery in the housing market that increased the collection of capital gains tax.
Most other tax categories logged a modest increase, with the collections of corporate tax, inheritance and gift tax, and individual consumption tax rising 0.1 trillion won each.
Meanwhile, the transportation, energy and environment tax decreased 0.3 trillion won, reflecting the government's decision to expand fuel tax cuts. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The purchasing managers' index (PMI) for China's non-manufacturing sector came in at 49 in August, unchanged from the level in July, official data showed on Monday.
The sub-index for business activity in the service sector stood at 49.3 in August, also flat from the previous month, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
As an indicator of macroeconomic trends, a PMI reading above 50 indicates expansion while a reading below 50 signals contraction.
By sector, the business activity indices for postal services, telecommunications, broadcasting, television and satellite transmission services, as well as internet, software and information technology services all remained above 55, indicating robust growth in business volume.
The business expectation index for the service sector stood at 55.5 in August, indicating a strong outlook for positive market developments.
The sub-index for business activity in the construction sector dropped 0.1 percentage points to 46.9 this month, the data revealed. NBS chief statistician Huo Lihui said construction activity slowed in some regions due to extreme weather, including heavy rains and typhoons.
The business expectation index for the construction sector remained flat at 51.8.
Monday's data also showed that the PMI for China's manufacturing sector stood at 49.8 in August, up 0.6 percentage points from July. The composite PMI output index rose from 49.3 to 49.5. ■

Seoul district offers foreigners multilingual help to navigate South Korean rental market
The foreign population in Gangbuk has nearly doubled over the past decade to roughly 7,000 residents
To help bridge this informational divide and protect vulnerable foreign renters, Gangbuk, a northern administrative district in Seoul, is expanding a comprehensive municipal programme designed to safeguard foreign residents throughout the housing lease process.
Under the enhanced initiative, foreign tenants visiting local neighbourhood centres to register their move-in address or file for an official “fixed date” status (hwakjeong ilja) will receive automated administrative guidance stamped directly onto their documentation in nine languages. The legal stamp – covering English, Chinese, Vietnamese, Mongolian, Tagalog, Uzbek, Japanese, Taiwanese and Thai – outlines essential protections under the Housing Lease Protection Act.
In the South Korean rental market, obtaining an official fixed date is a critical statutory step that grants tenants legal priority to reclaim key security deposits should a landlord face foreclosure or property auction.
Alongside the multilingual stamps, district offices are distributing QR code stickers linking directly to My Seoul, a dedicated mobile application operated by the Seoul Metropolitan Government. By scanning the code, foreign residents can easily install the application to access multi-language housing guidelines, municipal safety updates and multicultural social services.

Sri Lanka’s New Anti-Terrorism Legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:09:00 UTC
12:09:00 KST

Sri Lanka’s Cabinet has approved a bill to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) of 1979. The official Cabinet decision calls the replacement the “Safeguarding the State from Terrorism” Bill, while the government’s December 2025 consultation draft uses the term “Protection of the State from Terrorism.”
The National People’s Power (NPP) government has not given any reason yet for the change of name of the proposed legislation. It will be published in the Gazette and then presented to Parliament.
The Cabinet-approved text has not yet been made public. The only version that can presently be examined is the 2025 December draft, but it is unlikely that the bill will be significantly different from the draft, given the extensive consultations that followed the December draft.
The 2025 December draft is an improvement over the PTA of 1979. It attempts to define terrorism and related preparatory offenses more narrowly than the PTA did. It also contains safeguards that were absent or weaker under the PTA. For example, the draft recognizes access to counsel, requires notification of detention, provides for magistrates and the Human Rights Commission to visit detention facilities, and requires a detainee held under a detention order to be produced before a magistrate every 14 days. It restricts the use of statements made in custody — an important departure from the PTA’s admission of confessions made to senior police officers. A February 2026 assessment by United Nations experts acknowledged these improvements.
However, the December 2025 draft does not curb the exceptional executive power that critics of the PTA want. Under the December draft, the defense secretary can still renew two-month detention orders for a year. When a detention order is produced, the magistrate is expected to approve it, rather than decide independently whether the evidence justifies continued custody. The president may proscribe organizations and impose curfews, while the armed forces and Coast Guard receive powers normally associated with the police.
The government has not explained why it chose “Safeguarding the State from Terrorism,” as a title for the proposed law. But a law framed around safeguarding “the state” probably looks at protecting aspects such as sovereignty, territorial integrity, government institutions, and public order.
Sri Lanka has legitimate security interests and needs counterterror laws. It fought the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) for decades. At one point, the LTTE controlled about one-third of Sri Lanka’s territory. More recently, the 2019 Easter Sunday attackers targeted civilians and hotels, killing 269 people. But the attack also challenged the state’s capacity to detect and deter transnational ideological threats.
The December draft brings all these interests together. Some of its provisions criminalize the collection or supply of broadly defined “confidential information” that may affect national security and defense. Executive proscription, curfew, and the power the police still wields reinforce the state-security character of the law.
Cabinet spokesman Nalinda Jayatissa said the bill would cover terrorism “including organized crimes.” If that formulation appears in the final text, Parliament should ask whether the law is defining a distinct offense or simply extending counterterrorism powers to difficult forms of ordinary crime.
Sri Lanka nevertheless needs a preventive counterterrorism capacity. The Penal Code can punish crime like murder after the act. But terrorist attacks must be interrupted earlier. The state must act when would-be perpetrators are financing an operation, acquiring weapons, training recruits, selecting targets, or coordinating across borders.
These needs have grown more complex since 1979, when Sri Lanka enacted its first anti-terrorism law amid the looming threat posed by the LTTE. For example, the internet allows small groups to access information and technical knowledge from like-minded individuals based abroad. Terrorist financing can move through digital assets today and is better hidden than in the past.
The December draft recognizes some of this change. It reaches preparatory conduct, financing, transnational activity, and digital communications. It provides judicial authorization for interception and compelled decryption. These focus more on disruption than after-the-fact arrest and confession.
Custody still remains the main debating point of anti-terrorism legislation in the country. Counterterrorism investigations take time, and the complexity of these operations justify more investigative time. However, prolonged custody does not automatically lead to success against terrorism.
The PTA was fully operational when suicide bombers in 2019 killed more than 260 people. A parliamentary investigation and the presidential commission of inquiry found that officials had received specific warnings but failed to evaluate, share, and act on them. The state possessed extensive arrest and detention powers. What it lacked was institutional capacity to disrupt the attacks.
However, the 2025 December draft does not establish how intelligence agencies should share information, how competing warnings should be assessed, who is responsible for acting on them, or how intelligence should be converted into evidence that can survive trial. Those are matters of institutional design, resources and accountability as much as law.
One improvement over the 1979 law that the 2025 draft provides for is limiting the use of confessions made to the police as evidence. The question is whether the final bill creates conditions for financial, communications, and forensic evidence to replace confession-centered investigations, or merely adds safeguards around the old model.
The bill should therefore be judged by whether it is somewhat more liberal than the PTA. Once the Cabinet-approved text is gazetted, three questions will matter. Has the definition separated terrorist violence from protest, organized crime, and political advocacy? Can a court examine the basis for continued detention rather than simply record an executive decision? And does the law help institutions convert intelligence into timely disruption and prosecutable evidence?
Sri Lanka’s history shows why preventive powers are necessary. It also shows that locking people up for extended periods is not the same as prevention. A law designed to safeguard the state should strengthen the state’s ability to recognize and stop a credible threat.
The NPP government has an opportunity to move Sri Lanka away from a system that measures security through arrests and years spent in custody. The better test is whether the law helps the authorities disrupt credible threats and build cases that survive in court. A law that cannot turn intelligence into evidence will reproduce the central weakness of the PTA, regardless of how much power it gives the state.

Days before this report, 27 students fell ill after eating their mid-day meal.A Public Works Department survey of Kota district’s 1,088 govt schools found 61 buildings entirely ruined and marked for demolition, plus two classrooms flagged as unsafe in each of 318 school buildings, and one classroom each in a further 98. Only 41 full buildings and 29 partial structures have been demolished so far.District collector Peeyush Samaria’s office has no record of any personal inspection visit to a govt school. Samaria remained unavailable for comment. Sanganer, Jaipur: The CM’s constituency
Bhajan Lal Sharma won the Sanganer assembly constituency in 2023
At Bojyawas Govt Primary School, there are toilets, but they have no water. The water tank has cracked and dense cobwebs, indicating it hasn’t been in use for some time. The school shares space with a sub-health centre, where fungus covers medicine boxes and water stains mark chairs and registers.A staff member said open defecation has become routine for her. She does her best by consciously holding off the urge to use a toilet. The school itself has 10 students in classes 1 to 5 under a single teacher.
Govt Secondary School, Kalyanpura, looks well-kept from the gate, till you learn that one of its two buildings has been shut as unsafe, leaving 404 students across classes 1–12 to squeeze into four rooms.The school runs two shifts, 7am–12 noon and 12:30–6pm, and some second-shift students sit under a tin shed outside because the classes can’t accommodate them. Washrooms don’t have regular water supply and are cleaned only twice a month, said a Class 12 student.With no security guard and a broken, low boundary wall, the campus has seen repeated thefts. As a result, each classroom door has three latches and three separate locks.At Govt Upper Primary Sanskrit School in Hasampur Basdi, 85 students from classes 1 to VIII are taught in four classrooms — one of which is assigned to a booth level officer for special intensive revision (SIR) work.
Teacher Rajendra Verma produced letters he has submitted seeking a playground, boundary fencing and a tubewell. The school has been running on tanker water for close to a year, he said.At Govt Primary School in Hasampura, there was no need to interview anyone about the school’s condition. The gate was locked at 9.30am on a weekday. Former ward councillor Ram Singh Choudhary said he has been writing to govt for three years about the school’s lack of facilities. Jaisalmer & Barmer: Studying under treesIn Rajasthan’s desert border districts, several schools have no building.In Ramsar panchayat, Barmer, Govt Upper Primary School Azad Nagar was sanctioned in the 2022–23 budget and began classes in March 2023. But its 37 students study in a hut built by villagers or under trees.“Whether it rains, there is a storm or it is extremely hot, we have to study under trees,” said a Class V student.Land for the school was allotted only in 2024, and construction funds await sanction.At the Govt Higher Secondary School in Majal village, Samdari block (Balotra district), students and parents locked the school gate after nine teachers were transferred out at once, leaving senior secondary arts, science and agriculture streams without lecturers.“When there are no lecturers in the school, how will we study? How can Grade-II teachers perform the duties of lecturers?” a student asked.The protest ended after education officials agreed to post three teachers on deputation.Assembly data, drawn from UDISE 2025-26 figures, shows both districts have building-less schools: 36 in Barmer and 25 in Jaisalmer. Jaisalmer also features among districts hit hardest by a separate supply failure — a shortfall in the milk powder needed for the state’s Pannadhay Bal Gopal Yojana. Jhalawar: After 7 deaths, wait on for a new buildingOn the morning of July 25, 2025, the roof of Govt Upper Primary School in Piplodi, a tribal village in Jhalawar, collapsed during class hours. Seven children died; 21 were injured.A year on, Piplodi has visibly changed — better roads, more power connections, regular health camps, rising enrolment — but the one thing it still lacks is a functioning school building.Classes at the school have run since last August out of the two-room house of Mor Singh, a 60-year-old farmer and shepherd who vacated his own home so children would not lose another year of school.A new school building — eight classrooms, an anganwadi centre and a kitchen — is under construction, originally due by July 24, 2026. It has since been delayed after villagers raised concerns about construction quality when work began last November. Officials demolished the substandard work and restarted.“Construction of the school is taking longer than expected as villagers raised concerns about the quality of construction,” said Jhalawar collector Ajay Singh, adding that surprise inspections are now held every few weeks and the building should be ready by October.
Among Rajasthan’s blocks, Jhalawar has the highest concentration of building-less govt schools. District-wide, 81 schools lack toilets.Assembly data show 611 govt schools statewide with no building of their own, including 10 girls’ schools, 2,047 schools with buildings that lack toilets, and 1,049 that lack drinking water. It’s not that govt doesn’t spend on educationRajasthan’s 2026–27 budget allocates Rs 64,205 crore to school and college education. Of this allocation, around 75% goes into staff salaries and only 10–15% goes infrastructure.The state employs the second-highest number of teachers in the country, at 7.93 lakh, second only to UP. Yet, it has 7,200 single-teacher govt schools serving over 1.5 lakh students. Around 1.5 lakh sanctioned teacher posts remain vacant.The state’s own infrastructure data lays out the scale of the problem: 3,768 school buildings, 83,783 classrooms and 16,765 toilets are classified as entirely dilapidated while another 2,19,902 classrooms and 29,753 toilets need repair.Over the past two years, govt says it has spent Rs 2,723 crore building 179 new school buildings and 7,945 new classrooms to replace dilapidated ones.With govt funds in scarce supply, state-run schools increasingly lean on voluntary and community money. Statewide, philanthropic donations for school development totalled Rs 138 crore in 2024 and Rs 140 crore in 2025.In Pali district, a donor-led ‘Aao Gaon Chalen’ campaign — connecting migrants and philanthropists to their native villages — has targeted raising Rs 300 crore for infrastructure work.“There are around 23,000 such teachers in the state who are posted in a school where they are not needed, and their posting should be in another school, but they have not accepted their new posting. For instance, in an English-medium school, a Hindi-medium teacher who was earlier posted does not accept their new posting after a transfer, and the Hindi medium school, where the teacher is needed, students are suffering in that school,” said Mahendra Pandey, chief general secretary of Rajasthan Primary and Secondary Teachers Association.
TOI Special Report from Rajasthan
Gen Z, Gen alpha protestsThe consequences have spilled onto the streets.In Sikar, Class 12 students protested dilapidated buildings that force school closures every time it rains, alongside a shortage of subject teachers.In Gangapur City (Sawai Madhopur), girls locked the gates of the Mahatma Gandhi English Medium School in Meena Badoda, Wazirpur, after the principal was pulled onto local-body election duty, compounding an existing teacher shortage.At Govt Senior Secondary School in Majal village in Balotra district, students locked the gates after nine teachers were transferred simultaneously.A Class XII student at Govt Higher Secondary School at Majal in Balotra said: “If we had to study without teachers, then we could have studied at home. What is the need to come to school? If a school is operational, teachers must be posted.”
TOI Ground Report
The infrastructure debate has become an open political fight.A civic campaign, ‘School Thik Karo’, backed by CJP, has sent volunteer teams to inspect schools across nine districts — Jaipur, Ajmer, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Dholpur, Bharatpur, Kota, Barmer and Hanumangarh — after receiving what it says are public requests.“It has been over a year since the school collapse tragedy in Jhalawar, and the education minister has still not shared a concrete plan on how over 80,000 classrooms in dilapidated conditions will be fixed. Students are being forced to study in unsafe buildings, risking their lives,” said CJP national spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.One inspection, in Jaipur’s Bagru constituency, found a school that had been operating out of a buffalo shed for two and a half years after its own building was declared unsafe; it was shifted to a house only after drawing media attention.
The state education department has now issued an order requiring prior permission for any outsider to enter school premises, and barring photography, videography, interviews or livestreaming involving students without the principal’s consent.
Opposition leader Tikaram Jully called it an attempt to hide failures: “Instead of fixing schools, if you introduce ‘no entry’ measures just to hide your own failures, how can such accidents be prevented? A useless ‘double-engine’ govt,” Jully said.Additional reporting by Vimal Matta, Suparna Roy, Somdutt Trtpathi, Suntl Parmuwal & Shoeb Khan

U.S. Strikes Iran in First Military Action in a Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:05:16 UTC
12:05:16 KST

President Donald Trump vowed on Monday that the U.S. will strike Iran “hard” after the two countries exchanged their first publicly confirmed attacks in weeks.
Trump told Fox News’ Trey Yingst that “there will be a response” to strikes Iran launched against U.S. forces in Jordan overnight in retaliation for an American attack on an island in the Strait of Hormuz.
“We're going to hit them hard,” the President said, according to Yingst.
Trump’s threat comes after U.S. forces attacked two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island on Sunday, marking a resumption of military action after a roughly month-long pause.
CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the strike in a statement to TIME, adding that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces “were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” into the strait.
Last week, U.S. forces finished clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
“U.S. forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” Hawkins added.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) issued a statement soon after the U.S. strikes that was carried by Iranian state news agency IRNA, saying that Iran would respond to the attacks on Larak Island “with punishment for the aggressor.”
The IRGC later said in a statement early Monday local time that it had launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. air base in Jordan and warned that “every shot will be met with more devastating responses,” IRNA reported. Jordan’s armed forces said they intercepted eight missiles that entered the country’s airspace early Monday morning.
In a statement, CENTCOM rebuffed the Revolutionary Guards’ claims, describing the Sunday attack as “limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat” to the strait.
A pause in attacks
Before the Sunday strikes, the last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, announcing a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of IRGC targets in Iran, including command centers, missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defense sites.
On Aug. 1, President Donald Trump said that he agreed to “hold off” strikes in Iran at the request of the U.S.’s regional allies in the Middle East.
How the U.S.-Iran war began
The strikes mark the latest escalation in the war, which began on Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched a wave of attacks across Iran. Trump described the operation as a “massive and ongoing” campaign intended to eliminate what he called imminent threats from the Iranian regime and openly encouraged Iranians to overthrow their government.
The attacks came after U.S.-Iranian negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program failed to produce an agreement and amid the Iranian government’s deadly crackdown on nationwide protests. Trump had accused Iran of rebuilding its nuclear capabilities following U.S. and Israeli strikes on three major Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025. Iran has consistently denied seeking a nuclear weapon.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening salvo of the Feb. 28 campaign. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at Israel, U.S. military bases and other sites across the Middle East, widening the conflict throughout the region.
The war also led Iran to militarize and largely close the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy transit routes, through which about a fifth of global oil production typically passed before the hostilities.
A U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports was lifted under a June agreement, but Trump reimposed it after that deal and its accompanying cease-fire fell apart.
